Executive summary

This document records what 20 Texas Democrats have said and done on public education. Six of them have served in the Legislature, and all six voted against the 2025 education savings account law at every recorded House and Senate floor stage. On charter schools the 20 split. Teacher organizations backed every one of them who ran in 2026 and is not a judge: Texas AFT endorsed all 14, and the Texas State Teachers Association endorsed all but four. There doesn't appear to be a public record of a statement on teacher residencies from any of the 20.

The 20 are:

  • James Talarico, the U.S. senator-elect.
  • Seven statewide executive winners: Gina Hinojosa for governor, Vikki Goodwin for lieutenant governor, Nathan Johnson for attorney general, Sarah Eckhardt for comptroller, Benjamin Flores for land commissioner, Clayton Tucker for agriculture commissioner and Jon Rosenthal for railroad commissioner.
  • Four Texas Supreme Court winners: Maggie Ellis, Chari Kelly, Kristen Hawkins and Gisela D. Triana.
  • Five winners for the State Board of Education, the elected 15-member board that sets curriculum standards and approves teaching materials: Thomas Ray Garcia, Coretta Mallet-Fontenot, Allison Bush, Michelle Palmer and Tiffany Clark.
  • Dana Van de Walker, whose board race is not called.
  • Marisa B. Pérez-Díaz and Gustavo Reveles, sitting board Democrats who were not on the ballot.

The six who have served in the Legislature each voted no on Senate Bill 2 of 2025 at every recorded floor stage: Hinojosa, Goodwin, Talarico and Rosenthal in the House, and Johnson and Eckhardt in the Senate. The law created the state's education savings accounts, state money a family can spend on private-school costs. Eckhardt, who as comptroller will run the program, pledged in The Texan to "audit the daylights out of" it.

The voucher statements we found for the others who are not judges oppose public money for private-school tuition, though there doesn't appear to be a public record of Clark or Van de Walker addressing vouchers in their own words. Two statements are qualified, Bush's and, from among the six legislators, Hinojosa's. Bush's campaign FAQ says public funds "including vouchers" must strengthen classrooms, and it does not call for repeal. And under a child-care heading, a Texas Tribune guide carried by HPPR reported Hinojosa as saying vouchers "should be expanded to include public pre-K programs", without saying which vouchers it meant.

Hinojosa has pledged to replace Commissioner of Education Mike Morath with an educator, and in 2021 she filed a bill to make the commissioner an elected office. That bill was House Bill 613. The pledge is on her campaign site, and in her victory speech, as her campaign's transcript records it, she said, "on day one, I will fire Mike Morath". But no nominee has been named yet, as the Texas Tribune shows.

There doesn't appear to be a public record of any statement from her on appointments to the State Board for Educator Certification, the governor-appointed board that writes teacher-certification rules and is separate from the elected State Board of Education.

Talarico wrote in 2022 that high-quality nonprofit public charter schools have a role, but others here have asked for fewer new charters or a pause: Goodwin, Rosenthal, Mallet-Fontenot, Palmer, Van de Walker and Reveles. He wrote of "a role for high-quality nonprofit public charter schools" in a candidate survey on Teach the Vote, the site of the Association of Texas Professional Educators, a teacher association that runs the survey and does not endorse candidates.

Pérez-Díaz called for "a halt to the expansion" in 2018 and later voted to allow several new charters. On the board, Clark and Reveles voted against allowing every applicant on a named roll call in 2025 and 2026 except Unidos Soccer Leadership Academy. Each voted to allow that school and then voted not to veto it.

The four who served in the House split on House Bill 4545 of 2021, but all four voted against House Bill 8 of 2025, the law that replaced the state test, and so did Johnson. House Bill 4545 dealt with retakes and extra instruction for students who fail the state test, STAAR. Talarico voted no on it in committee and then yes at every House floor vote. Goodwin and Rosenthal voted no throughout, and Hinojosa voted no and then yes on the final version.

Texas AFT, the Texas affiliate of the national American Federation of Teachers, endorsed all 14 non-judicial 2026 candidates here, and only Talarico has 2026 backing from a reform group. The Texas State Teachers Association endorsed all of them except Flores, Tucker, Rosenthal and Mallet-Fontenot. Talarico's reform backing comes from Democrats for Education Reform, a national group that endorses Democratic candidates.

Among direct contributions, Hinojosa received the largest from teacher organizations that we identified: $250,000 from the American Federation of Teachers' national committee and $250,000 from the National Education Association's. Larger sums are reported to have gone to outside groups supporting Talarico, not to his campaign. The Houston Chronicle reported that Reed Hastings gave $1,000,000 to outside groups supporting him, though the Chronicle did not name the receiving committee. The Texas Tribune reported that Stephen Mandel gave $500,000 to Lone Star Rising PAC, a super PAC (a type of political action committee) that operates independently of his campaign.

The Republican opponents had education-oriented backers of their own. The Texas Home School Coalition, a home-school advocacy group, endorsed the Republican opponent in each of the 12 statewide races in this document: the U.S. Senate race, the seven executive offices and the four Supreme Court seats. It also endorsed three Republican State Board candidates, Victoria Hinojosa in District 2, Tiffany Nelson in District 6 and Audrey Young in District 8. Charter Schools Now PAC, a charter-school political committee, endorsed Greg Abbott, Hinojosa's opponent, and funded four Republican State Board candidates.

There doesn't appear to be a public record of statements on education policy by the four judges, Ellis, Kelly, Hawkins and Triana, in the sources we could open. The Code of Judicial Conduct bars pledges suggesting how they would decide classes of cases.

What they have on record is rulings, among them Triana's 2020 opinion upholding an injunction that the Houston Independent School District won against the commissioner of education's takeover steps. In that takeover, announced in 2019, the state replaced the district's elected board with "an agency-run board of managers", in the words of Teach the Vote. The Supreme Court later reversed and vacated the injunction, noting that the Legislature had since rewritten the governing law.

Implications for the future

On most education questions the Democratic winners want the same things, and in 2027 we expect them to act through the offices they won. There will be few new education laws. Every new law needs the Senate, and Republicans are projected to keep it. So the first changes will come through who runs the state agencies and through the budget, which both parties must agree on.

The voucher program stays, but its funding for 2028 and 2029 is undecided

The Legislature is very unlikely to repeal the 2025 voucher law in the session that ends in May 2027. That law created education savings accounts, state money that families can spend on private-school costs. All six winners who served in the Legislature voted against it, and Hinojosa, the governor-elect, pledged to end it. But repeal would have to pass the Senate, where Republicans passed the law in 2025 and are projected to keep their majority.

A comparable case points the same way. In Arizona, Governor Katie Hobbs tried in her first year to repeal the universal part of her state's program, and the attempt failed against Republican lawmakers. In Texas the first sign will be what happens to the six repeal bills filed on November 9, 2026, none of which is yet in committee.

Meanwhile the program will be run by one of the six who voted against it. As comptroller, Eckhardt will be the statewide official who administers the voucher program and also estimates the state's revenue. She will very likely keep the program running through the 2026-27 school year and audit it by August 2027, as she pledged.

Money for the program in 2028 and 2029 is a separate question. Whether the budget settled by June 2027 includes it is uncertain, because House budget writers, the governor and the Senate all shape that budget.

The 2025 teacher raises keep their funding, and a new raise is uncertain

The teacher raises in the 2025 school finance law will very likely stay funded in the budget settled by June 2027. Current law already requires districts to keep paying them. Each winner who voted on that law voted for it at least once, and the Senate passed it 31 to 0.

The same vote shows that the Senate is not a known opponent of raises. Even so, whether a new across-the-board raise becomes law by June 2027 is uncertain. Hinojosa pledged higher teacher pay but named no dollar figure, and the open questions are money and what each chamber asks in return.

The money will become clearer in January 2027, with the comptroller's revenue estimate, because spending bills normally must fit within the money the comptroller says the state will have. The House's first budget follows.

Hinojosa's choice likely runs the education agency, and the 2025 testing law stays

Hinojosa's choice for commissioner of education will likely be running the Texas Education Agency, which oversees public schools, by May 2027, either confirmed or serving while the Senate decides. Whether the Senate confirms that nominee by May 2027 is uncertain. On projected results, confirmation needs at least nine Republican senators if every senator votes.

The Legislature is very unlikely to cancel the 2025 testing law's tests or pause the A to F ratings, the state's letter grades for schools, by August 2028. The Senate passed that law 21 to 5. A pause without a new law is also very unlikely by then, since the testing law requires ratings every year, with listed exceptions. What a commissioner can change is the standards or measures behind the ratings, and if Hinojosa's choice is in office, we think that change likely by August 2028.

In Houston, a state-appointed board of managers replaced the elected school board, and Hinojosa pledged to restore the elected board. In a May 2025 letter, the current commissioner promised to announce a timeline on or around June 1, 2027, so that announcement will very likely come by the end of 2027. Elected trustees are very unlikely to hold every seat by then.

No charter pause becomes law, and more State Board vetoes are uncertain

A binding pause on new charter schools is very unlikely to become law by May 2027. Like every new law, it would have to pass the Senate.

The people covered here are split on charters, the publicly funded schools run under a state charter. Talarico, the U.S. senator-elect, wrote in 2022 that high-quality nonprofit charters have a role. Goodwin and Rosenthal asked for fewer new charters or a pause, and so did four Democrats who sit on or ran for the State Board of Education, the elected 15-member board that sets curriculum.

That board can veto a new charter the commissioner proposes, and whether it vetoes more of them by the end of 2027 is uncertain. Its Democrats have not voted the same way on charters. Two Democratic members voted against nearly every applicant in 2025 and 2026, while a third voted to allow several. The parties hold seven seats each, and District 8, the one board race not yet called, decides which party has eight. The final count there, due by December 7, 2026, will settle that question.

The Ten Commandments law stays, but the attorney general likely stops arguing for it in court

The 2025 Ten Commandments law requires the commandments to be displayed in classrooms. Hinojosa and Johnson voted against it, but the Legislature is very unlikely to repeal it by May 2027, because repeal needs the Senate. Repeal of the 2023 and 2025 laws on school library books is also very unlikely by then.

What can change is how the state defends the law. Johnson will be attorney general, the official who represents the state in appeals, and as a candidate he said he would not defend the law because he considers it unconstitutional. His office will likely stop arguing for it in court by the end of 2027. That would not repeal the law, and schools must still comply unless a court blocks it.

The State Board's 2026 social studies standards and its reading list with Bible stories stay unless a board majority votes to reopen them. Whether it does so by the end of 2027 is uncertain, and it depends on who wins District 8.

Teacher certification rules likely stay as they are, and preparation funding continues

The rules for preparing and certifying teachers are unlikely to change substantially by the end of 2027. There doesn't appear to be a public record of a pledge from Hinojosa that names a certification rule, program or funding source, or of a statement from any of the 20 people covered here on teacher residencies, routes built around a supervised year in a classroom before certification.

That silence is not evidence that nothing will change. The governor appoints the voting members of the State Board for Educator Certification, the board that writes the rules, and the Senate must consent, so the estimate depends on who sits on that board in 2027. A third of its seats expire on February 1, 2027, and Hinojosa's nominees for them will show which way the rules move.

The money for preparing teachers is another matter. The 2025 school finance law included money for teacher preparation programs, and the budget settled by June 2027 will very likely fund it as designed for 2028 and 2029. Every winner who voted on that law voted for it at least once, and there doesn't appear to be a public record of any group opposing the funding.

The 2023 and 2025 university laws stay through the 2027 session

Repeal of either the 2023 law on university diversity offices or the 2025 law on faculty governance is very unlikely by May 2027. Here too, repeal needs the Senate.

Regents govern the state's public university systems, and Hinojosa plans to appoint regents who would extend tuition grants to housing, food, transportation and textbooks. We make no estimate on those appointments, because we found too few comparable cases. A number of regents' seats expire in February 2027, which makes it the month to watch; news reports put the number of expiring seats at 11 or 20.

The estimates at a glance

Our firmest estimates are about what one office can do alone or what current law already requires. Of the 20 events in the table, we rate four very likely, three likely (one of them only if a commissioner Hinojosa chose is in office), five uncertain, one unlikely and seven very unlikely. Five of the seven very unlikely events are new laws or repeals, and each would have to pass the Senate.

Dates to watch

  • December 7, 2026: the official count ends and should settle State Board District 8, where the Democrat Dana Van de Walker led by 564 votes in the state's count of November 4. The result affects our estimates on charter vetoes and on reopening the curriculum.
  • January 2027: the Senate votes on its rules. Republicans will likely use that vote, by January 31, 2027, to cut the lieutenant governor's power over committees and bills. The lieutenant governor presides over the Senate, and if Vikki Goodwin, who takes that office, keeps those powers, every estimate that needs the Senate becomes less firm.
  • January 2027: the comptroller's revenue estimate sets how much lawmakers can normally spend. Our estimates on voucher funding, a new teacher raise and teacher-preparation money all depend on it.
  • January to May 2027: the Senate votes on Hinojosa's nominee for commissioner. That vote affects four estimates: who runs the agency, confirmation, the ratings and charter vetoes.
  • On or around June 1, 2027: the commissioner promised to announce a timeline for Houston's school board. Both Houston estimates depend on that announcement.

These are our estimates as of November 9, 2026, and no source offers odds. The rules, sources and reasoning behind each one are in the section "How we made the estimates" under Sources and method.

Teacher preparation and certification across the slate

The State Board for Educator Certification writes Texas's teacher-certification rules, and the elected State Board of Education may reject them but may not change them. Under chapter 21 of the Education Code, the certification board writes the rules for certificates and for the programs that prepare teachers, and the governor appoints its 11 voting members with Senate consent, plus two nonvoting members, one of them from an alternative preparation program. Every rule the certification board proposes then goes to the State Board of Education, which under §21.042 may reject it by a two-thirds vote of members present and voting within 90 days, but may not change it.

In June 2026 the State Board let the rules carrying out House Bill 2, the 2025 school-funding law, take effect on a consent calendar, a set of items approved together in a single vote, and its minutes of June 26, 2026 record no individual votes. That package covered the routes into teaching. The committee minutes of June 25, 2026 list its parts: admission to preparation programs, new preparation routes set up by House Bill 2, and intern and aide certificates.

Districts can also avoid some of these rules. Teach the Vote, the candidate-information site of the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, says the Districts of Innovation law lets a district exempt itself from some state requirements, including rules on hiring certified teachers.

The largest alternative-certification provider, A+ Texas Teachers, also known as Texas Teachers of Tomorrow, was in litigation with the Texas Education Agency and the certification board in 2023 and 2024 over its compliance with an agreed order. The case was before the Third Court of Appeals in Austin.

Seventeen of the 20 have a record on teacher preparation or certification, set out in the table below. There doesn't appear to be a public record of the other three, Benjamin Flores, Maggie Ellis and Kristen Hawkins, on the subject.

17 rows

One question recurs across the record: who should control certification rules. Johnson offered the 2023 amendment to keep the State Board of Education's power to reject them, and Eckhardt voted for it. It failed, 12 to 19.

On ATPE's Teach the Vote, Bush and Pérez-Díaz have said the board should keep that power, and Palmer prefers the elected board to the appointed one. Garcia would give the board power to amend the rules, which the law now forbids.

The other recurring subject is uncertified teachers. Hinojosa has addressed them, and so have Goodwin, Rosenthal, Mallet-Fontenot, Van de Walker, Pérez-Díaz and Reveles. Of these, only Reveles has said they should be allowed in some cases, in a 2024 League of Women Voters guide. Johnson cited the state's figure in his 2024 survey answer on Teach the Vote: 28.8 percent of new teachers hired in 2022-23 were uncertified.

For the four judges, the finding is that there doesn't appear to be a public record of teacher-organization backing. The Texas AFL-CIO, a labor federation that includes teacher-union affiliates, endorsed all four on July 21, 2026, but that is a labor endorsement rather than an education one.

In an earlier election cycle, for the Third Court of Appeals, an Austin law firm with school-district and higher-education practices gave Kelly $1,030 and Triana $1,000 on November 27, 2023.

Education-oriented groups also backed the opponents. Two releases from the campaign of Greg Abbott, Hinojosa's opponent, name two such groups. Charter Schools Now PAC endorsed him, and the American Federation for Children, a school-choice group, endorsed him on February 10, 2026.

The Texas Home School Coalition endorsed the Republican opponent in each of the 12 statewide races in this document. That meant Ken Paxton in the U.S. Senate race and, in the seven executive races, Greg Abbott, Dan Patrick, Mayes Middleton, Don Huffines, Dawn Buckingham, Nate Sheets and Bo French. For the four Supreme Court seats the coalition endorsed Jimmy Blacklock, James P. Sullivan, Kyle Hawkins and Brett Busby. It also endorsed three Republican State Board candidates:

  • Victoria Hinojosa, Garcia's opponent in District 2.
  • Tiffany Nelson, Palmer's opponent in District 6.
  • Audrey Young, Van de Walker's opponent in District 8.

Charter Schools Now PAC gave money to all three of those State Board candidates and to one more. Two campaign finance reports record $2,500 to Victoria Hinojosa, $1,000 to Tammie Nielsen, Mallet-Fontenot's opponent, and $2,500 plus $32,483 in in-kind ads to Tiffany Nelson. An earlier report records $5,000 to Audrey Young in April 2025.

The same committee also endorsed and funded Bush's Democratic runoff opponent, Stephanie Limon Bazan. And Commit to Students PAC, a Dallas committee whose purpose was not established, gave Dan Patrick $5,000.

Two groups that appear in the profiles do not endorse candidates. The Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, a teacher association, says on its ATPE-PAC page that its political committee's contributions "do not constitute a public endorsement by ATPE". That committee gave to Hinojosa's 2026 campaign for governor, Bush's 2026 State Board runoff campaign and Talarico's earlier Texas House campaigns, and those items appear here as contributions.

Raise Your Hand Texas, a public-education advocacy group, says on its website that it "will not endorse candidates". The Charles Butt Public Education PAC, which gave to Talarico's House campaigns, is a separate committee, and we did not establish a link between the two.

Texas Parent PAC, by contrast, does endorse candidates. In the 2026 primaries it endorsed only Hinojosa.

Statewide executive offices

Gina Hinojosa, Governor

The Associated Press called the race for Hinojosa over Greg Abbott, the incumbent, and the Texas Tribune's live results, which use Associated Press data, carry that call. The Texas Secretary of State's unofficial results show the count. The result is not certified. The state's official count, the canvass, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Hinojosa voted against the 2025 education savings account law at second and third reading in the House, and as a candidate she pledged to end the program.

The office she won appoints the commissioner of education, who runs the Texas Education Agency, and the voting members of the State Board for Educator Certification, which sets teacher-certification rules.

She comes to it from the Texas House, where she has served since 2017. On April 17, 2025, she voted no on Senate Bill 2, the voucher law, at second and third reading. Later that year she voted against House Bill 8, the 2025 testing law, at second reading, third reading and concurrence, and her campaign site pledges to end the state's standardized test.

The same campaign site calls her "a negotiator of the historic 2019 school finance bill," but Texas Legislature Online does not list her on that bill's conference committee.

In a 2024 letter, her most detailed statement on certification, she called for a reversal of the decline in certified teachers. There doesn't appear to be a public record of a pledge from her that names a certification rule, program or funding source, or of any statement from her, in coverage from November 4 to 6, 2026, on appointments to the certification board or on its rules.

Background and powers of the office

Hinojosa's first race was for the board of the Austin Independent School District, or Austin ISD, where she won an at-large seat in November 2012. The district's announcements of January 7, 2015 and December 14, 2015 date her time as board president from January 2015 to December 15, 2015. She gave up the presidency that day to run for the Texas House.

She left the board in November 2016 and has represented House District 49, in Austin, since January 10, 2017. On October 15, 2025, in Brownsville, she launched her campaign for governor.

  • Education roles. In 2019 she chaired the House Democratic Caucus Special Committee on Public Education, a working group of House Democrats. In the 88th Legislature, in 2023, she sat on the House Public Education Committee and on the Select Committee on Educational Opportunity & Enrichment, which was the House's 2023 interim committee on vouchers. Public Education's minutes of April 3, 2025 show her on the committee again in 2025.
  • The commissioner of education. The governor appoints the commissioner who runs the Texas Education Agency, or TEA, the state agency that oversees public schools. The Texas Tribune reported on November 5, 2026, that "Hinojosa must appoint someone and submit the name to the Texas Senate for official confirmation", and described that confirmation as needing a two-thirds vote.
  • Budget veto and the State Board of Education. According to the same Tribune article, the governor can veto single budget items, such as funding for the education savings account program, and names the chair of the elected State Board of Education from among its members.
  • Educator certification. The State Board for Educator Certification sets the rules for teacher certification and for the programs that prepare teachers, under chapter 21 of the Education Code. Under section 21.033, the governor appoints, with Senate consent, all 11 of its voting members: four public-school teachers, two administrators, one counselor and four citizens. The governor also appoints two nonvoting members, a dean of a college of education and a person from an alternative educator preparation program.

Record by issue

General notes

Social media

We read her Bluesky account, @ginafortexas.bsky.social, in full from November 2024 to November 5, 2026. She wrote 471 original posts there in that period, 128 of them on education, and all the posts below come from that account.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

She pledged to end the education savings account program. Her campaign site, on a page last modified August 11, 2026, says "Gina will end the voucher scam and ensure Texans' taxpayer dollars go where they belong".

The program, created by Senate Bill 2 in 2025, uses state money for private-school costs. At a September 2026 press conference she said, "We cannot afford to take $4 billion to give to this unaccountable voucher scam, so I will block that." The Texas Tribune printed those words on November 5, 2026.

On February 5, 2026, she told Austin PBS, "I believe we can undo vouchers." Her reason was that some House and Senate Republicans want to undo them but "do not feel free to vote their conscience".

Statement or interview

She opposed vouchers in each of these four statements, from 2016 to Election Day 2026:

  • In her 2016 ATPE survey on Teach the Vote, she wrote: "I will not support any proposal to create a voucher, or a neo-vouchers program in Texas."
  • On October 19, 2023, she said, "The Governor's bribe is immoral," in a Center Square story carried by the Washington Examiner. Abbott had offered to add teacher pay to a special session once education savings accounts passed.
  • In the final House debate on Senate Bill 2, on April 17, 2025, she said, "This bill is everything that is wrong with politics."
  • On Election Day, November 3, 2026, she cited her work with House Republicans as the model for her governorship: "In 2023, we stopped vouchers."

Social media

  • On February 6, 2025, she posted: "If 5.5M public school kids must take it, so should everyone in taxpayer-funded education, including wealthy families taking a voucher".
  • On January 16, 2026, she wrote that "every time they talk about 'school choice' they are actually taking options away from Texans".

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

She pledged higher teacher pay and more local control of district spending. Her campaign site promises to "audit and terminate" vendor contracts and to "use that money to pay teachers to be among the highest paid in the nation", without a dollar figure.

In her signed 2026 survey for the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, a teacher association that does not endorse candidates, she wrote on its Teach the Vote site: "I will also reinstate local control to allow districts more autonomy in how they spend their tax dollars."

Statement or interview

She has spoken on recapture, the 2019 school finance law and teacher base pay. Recapture is the system that sends part of property-wealthy districts' school taxes to the state, and as an Austin ISD trustee she described it in Spectrum News on May 10, 2016: "It's about $1,000 for the average property taxpayer in Austin that goes directly to the State of Texas to pay for public education elsewhere."

Statement or interview

  • The 2019 school finance law (House Bill 3). On April 3, 2019, she said of the bill, "To the teachers who dedicate their working lives to our kids, who for too long have been under-appreciated and unheard: We hear you, and this bill is for you." Her campaign site says "Gina was a negotiator of the historic 2019 school finance bill." Texas Legislature Online for the 86th Legislature does not list her on that bill's conference committee, and her own 2019 recap, in an archived newsletter, credited "the HB 3 conference committee members". It described her role as "heading up the House Democratic Caucus' Special Committee on Public Education".
  • In Spectrum News on June 2, 2026, she favored higher base pay over the Teacher Incentive Allotment, the state's performance-based teacher pay program: "We need to do something about base pay so that we can impact all teachers."

Social media

  • A post of January 28, 2025 on the basic allotment, the per-student base amount in the state formula, cited $1,340: "That's how much TX needs to increase basic allotment (per student funding) just to get back to 2019 spending power".
  • Of Texas teachers, she posted on October 22, 2025: "they should be among the best paid in the nation".

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

She pledged to end the state test, to give districts the state took over back to their communities and to replace the commissioner of education with an educator. Her campaign site says "Gina will end the STAAR test and tests like it, pause the rigged A-F accountability system, and call on the Legislature to deliver a bill that creates real accountability".

Texas Standard explained both terms on October 23, 2026. STAAR is the state's standardized test, written by TEA, and the A-F system is the letter grade the state assigns each school and district.

The same campaign page pledges, "Gina will return school districts that have been taken over back to their communities". It also pledges to replace Commissioner Mike Morath with an educator because "the agency that oversees our children's education should be led by someone who has taught them".

  • During STAAR testing week, on April 8, 2026, she said in a campaign release: "As governor, I will end this testing madness that is hurting our kids and destroying our neighborhood schools."
  • Speaking at Houston ISD, a district the state took over, on September 22, 2026, she said in another campaign release: "When I am governor, I will give Houston ISD back to the people of Houston, so that there can be accountability again."
  • Her victory speech on November 3, 2026, as the campaign's transcript records it, included "on day one, I will fire Mike Morath" and "your schools will not close."

Statement or interview

She has criticized test-based penalties, the state's 2023 conservatorship over Austin ISD and the 2025 testing law. In 2016 she wrote on Teach the Vote, "Testing should not be a punitive measure used to fire teachers or to close neighborhood schools."

When TEA appointed a conservator for Austin ISD over special education on March 31, 2023, she said, "I am dismayed by [TEA Commissioner Mike] Morath's decision to install a conservatorship in our school district at this time."

  • On House Bill 8, the 2025 testing law, she argued on August 26, 2025, that TEA "should not be in charge of creating the test." On September 3, 2025, the day of the House's last vote on the bill, she said, "This is no win. This is a terrible bill."
  • Her campaign site says, "Last year, she successfully reduced the number of STAAR tests our kids take." The record supports this for one test. Her House amendment cut the testing schedule to the federal minimum, but the Senate restored the other tests, and the enrolled bill drops only the English II end-of-course exam. The Tribune wrote that "Hinojosa added a provision to get rid of the English II test." She voted against the bill at second reading, third reading and concurrence with the Senate's version.
  • On October 23, 2026, she said of STAAR in Texas Standard: "It is created by the Texas Education Agency that then decides how to grade it after the kids have already taken the test." She added, "We need an objective outside measure of our kids' performance." Of Morath, she said in the same interview: "I don't have anything against the man personally, but I do believe we need an educator in that position to get us back on track."
  • On November 5, 2026, the Texas Tribune reported that "her team was "actively interviewing" people to replace Morath". No nominee was named.

Social media

  • On August 26, 2025, she posted: "the House adopted my amendment to cut the number of high stakes tests to the federal requirement".

Charter schools

Statement or interview

She has opposed charter takeovers of local schools and charter admission rules based on discipline history.

  • As a trustee in December 2012, she spoke on ending Austin ISD's contract with the IDEA charter network: "At some point so much damage is done that it's time for a divorce."
  • In her 2016 survey on Teach the Vote, she wrote: "I do not support allowing charter organizations, management companies, or an achievement authority to take over local schools."
  • Of her bill to bar charters from refusing students for discipline history, her 2019 newsletter said: "Public schools take all kids, and so should charter schools."
  • Her campaign site says she "passed legislation to ban charter schools from discriminating against kids because of their disciplinary record". Her own 2025 bill on this, House Bill 1179, did not advance out of committee. A 2025 discipline law by another author, House Bill 6, removed the "discipline problems" exclusion ground, though the enrolled House Bill 6 still allows exclusion of a student who "has been convicted of a criminal offense or has a juvenile court adjudication". She was neither an author nor a coauthor of House Bill 6, but she voted for it at House second and third reading.

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Statement or interview

She has spoken on critical race theory and on curriculum written by artificial intelligence. At a Texas Tribune event in November 2021, she called "critical race theory" "a made-up issue that is brilliantly used to polarize people". On September 22, 2026, speaking about curriculum generated by artificial intelligence in Houston ISD, she said in a campaign release: "I think that curriculum needs to be made by human beings."

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

Her campaign site says experienced teachers "are being replaced by uncertified first-time teachers", in a passage that ties teacher departures to pay, workload and STAAR.

Her campaign newsletter of August 24, 2026 said "we have to give new educators the support and mentorship they need to become great teachers". The same newsletter said she had "every intention of appointing an educator as head of TEA".

A month later, in a newsletter of September 23, 2026 written against instruction led by artificial intelligence, she wrote, "That means having certified teachers at the front of the classroom."

Statement or interview

Her most detailed statement is a signed letter of November 18, 2024, to Brad Buckley, chair of the Public Education Committee, printed as Appendix A of the House Committee on Public Education Interim Report 2024.

The appendix pages are scanned images, so the wording below comes from a text-recognition reading of them. In the letter, she wrote that uncertified teachers had "tripled in the last 10 years" and that:

  • "The Speaker's Interim Recommendations appropriately identify "teacher certification" as a goal of our work."
  • "reversing the alarming, precipitous decline of certified teachers in Texas public schools should be the priority of the upcoming legislative session."
  • "But compensation that is dependent in large part on testing performance is problematic"
  • "A qualified, professional teacher in the classroom is foundational to a quality education."

Her other statements on the subject include these:

  • In her 2016 survey on Teach the Vote, she wrote: "I do not support using student scores on state standardized tests in teacher evaluations."
  • As a trustee in October 2016, she asked that Austin ISD's pilots to reduce the number of ineffective teachers be built with Education Austin, the local teachers union. The Austin Monitor wrote: "Hinojosa asked for this measure to be developed hand-in-hand with Education Austin."
  • Her May 5, 2026 newsletter cited "an alarming 10 point decrease in the number of certified teachers since Greg Abbott has been governor", with no source for the figure.
  • She repeated the "uncertified first-time teachers" line in her August 14, 2026 newsletter, and a September 9, 2026 campaign email used "uncertified, first-time teachers".
  • A June 2, 2026, Spectrum News article that quoted her on base pay also stated that "House Bill 2 also banned the hiring of uncertified teachers". That description of the 2025 school-funding law is the reporter's, not hers.
  • Her certification bills and her amendment to a 2023 certification bill appear under "Voting record."

Social media

  • On May 4, 2026, she posted: "the best thing we can do for our kids is put a great teacher in the classroom".
  • On August 19, 2026, she wrote: "No governor in Texas history has driven more teachers away from the classroom than Greg Abbott".

Higher education

Campaign pledge

A Texas Tribune guide to affordability, which High Plains Public Radio republished on October 8, 2026, summarized her plan this way: "She wants to appoint university regents who would expand tuition grant programs to include housing, food, transportation and textbook costs." The guide added that she would have the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board, a state higher-education agency, investigate rising costs.

Statement or interview

In 2016 the Daily Texan reported that she "believes public universities should have the same right as private universities to opt out of campus carry".

Other

Campaign pledge

Under its "Childcare" heading, the same guide said she "told the Texas Tribune that Texas' vouchers should be expanded to include public pre-K programs". It did not say whether "vouchers" meant the education savings accounts or child-care subsidies. We did not find her full answer.

Statement or interview

Outside the Governor's Mansion on October 15, 2026, she named raising the purchase age for assault-style weapons to 21 as a school-safety priority after the Uvalde shooting: "That will be my priority. Out of decency for what was lost."

She had come to challenge Abbott to a debate, and, in ABC News 4's words, "Abbott did not make an appearance." No debate took place.

Voting record

She has voted on education bills on the House floor in every regular session since 2017, and the table lists her recorded votes from the House Journal.

On vouchers, she voted for the budget amendments of 2017, 2021 and 2023 that barred money for them, for the 2017 motion telling House negotiators on House Bill 21 not to adopt a voucher program, and for the amendment that struck the education savings account program from House Bill 1 in the fourth called session of 2023. She voted against Senate Bill 2 in 2025 at second and third reading.

She voted for House Bill 3 of 2019 and House Bill 2 of 2025, both school finance bills, at all three stages. But on eleven bills on curriculum, instructional materials, school libraries, religion in schools, parental rights and universities, she voted no at every stage at which she was present: House Bill 3979 and Senate Bill 3 of 2021, on teaching about race; House Bills 900 and 1605 and Senate Bills 763, 17 and 18 of 2023; and Senate Bills 10, 12, 13 and 37 of 2025. The one exception on those bills was her yes on Buckley Amendment 1 to Senate Bill 13.

Floor amendments she offered. She offered the amendments below to a 2023 teacher-certificate bill and to the 2025 voucher and Ten Commandments laws. Her amendment to House Bill 8 of 2025, the testing law, appears under "Public statements and interviews."

  • House Bill 621 of 2023 concerned a temporary teaching certificate for veterans without a bachelor's degree. Her Amendment 1 limited the certificate to career and technology education and cut its validity from five years to three, and the House adopted it on May 1, 2023.
  • On the same bill, the journal recorded her as voting no on sending it to third reading. She then filed a statement in the House Journal: "When Record No. 783 was taken, I was shown voting no. I intended to vote yes. Hinojosa"
  • Texas Legislature Online lists her as one of the House negotiators on the bill's conference committee. The enrolled bill covers "creating a temporary certification to teach career and technology education for certain military service members and first responders", valid for three years. She gave no stated reason for the amendment.
  • Her Amendment 18 to Senate Bill 2 of 2025 would have struck the option of "a nationally norm-referenced assessment instrument", so that students using education savings accounts would take the state test. It was tabled.
  • Her amendment to Senate Bill 10 of 2025, the Ten Commandments law, provided that "the state is liable for the expenses, costs, judgments, or settlements" of school lawsuits over compliance. It was adopted, and she then voted against the bill at second and third reading.

Education bills she authored. None of these became law as a standalone bill.

  • She filed a charter-admissions bill every session from 2017 to 2025. The last of them, House Bill 1179 of 2025, would have added "discipline history" to barred admission criteria. Two earlier ones, House Bill 43 of 2019 and House Bill 97 of 2021, cleared committee, but each stopped when the committee report was sent to the House Calendars Committee. Raise Your Hand Texas, a public-education advocacy group that does not endorse candidates, backed the 2021 bill in testimony in April 2021: "Raise Your Hand Texas supports House Bill 97 by Representative Hinojosa".
  • Her pay and funding bills include House Bill 3804 of 2019, an annual cost-of-living adjustment for district employees, and House Bill 4586 of 2023, raising the basic allotment to "$7,075". House Bill 177, filed in the 2023 third called session, proposed a "one-time bonus payment of $15,000" for teachers.
  • Two bills concerned TEA and its commissioner. House Bill 5419 of 2025 would have audited TEA contracts, capped its staffing and set as a funding priority "attaining and maintaining pay for classroom teachers of at least the national average". House Bill 613 of 2021 would have made the commissioner of education an elected office: "commissioner of education is elected by the qualified voters at the general election". Her 2026 pledge is to appoint an educator.
  • On teacher preparation, House Bill 4839 of 2023 would have added to the accountability standards for preparation programs the "quality of a candidate's implementation of the key components of a performance assessment identified by the board". It did not advance out of committee.
  • She coauthored House Bill 1276 of 2019. In districts of 5,000 or more students, no student in grades 1 to 6 could have been assigned two years in a row to a teacher with under one year of experience who "does not hold the appropriate certificate required under Section 21.003". The bill passed the House and did not pass the Senate.
  • Her House Bill 5282 of 2025 provided that "the agency shall prohibit the use of artificial intelligence" to score written test answers unless validated.

Austin ISD board votes, 2012 to 2016. As a trustee she cast recorded votes on the IDEA charter contract and on campus plans, and she moved a change to the district scorecard.

  • On December 17, 2012, she voted to end the district's contract with the IDEA charter network, which passed 5-4, and voted against an amendment to keep IDEA's grades 6 and 7 at Allan.
  • At the same meeting, the board, including her, "unanimously approved four Annual Academic and Facilities Recommendations". These included an in-district charter at Travis Heights started by the campus.
  • In June 2015, as president, she proposed raises of 3% for all employees in 2015-16 and 2% the next year.
  • On October 24, 2016, she moved to replace the post-secondary readiness standard with the passing standard in the district's scorecard, and the motion failed.
  • In 2026 she said on KUT of her board tenure, "We saved them. We didn't shut down any schools." We retrieved no Austin ISD roll call on school closures from 2012 to 2016 to check it.

Education-oriented backers

Teacher-organization endorsements. Texas AFT, the Texas affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers, endorsed her for the March 2026 primary and the general election. Its executive council approved the endorsement on December 6, 2025, and the organization announced it on December 9.

The Texas State Teachers Association, or TSTA, endorsed her for the primary on February 18, 2026 and kept her on its general-election list. Her campaign endorsements page also lists, without dates, three local teacher organizations: the Houston Federation of Teachers (the Houston teachers' union), the Alliance of Dallas Educators United Teachers and Aldine AFT Local 6345.

Teacher-organization money. Teacher organizations and their committees gave her the 19 contributions in the table below, all direct unless marked in-kind. The two largest came from national committees. The $250,000 from "American Federation of Teachers COPE" on August 5, 2026, listed in her report, came from the national union's committee, not the Texas affiliate. The National Education Association's committee gave a separate $250,000.

Texas AFT's own committee gave $10,000, $25,000 and $50,000 in cash and $9,959 in kind, as its committee reports show, among them those covering March to May 2026 and May to June 2026. Statewide executive offices

Vikki Goodwin, Lieutenant Governor

The Associated Press called the race for Goodwin over Dan Patrick, the incumbent, as the Texas Tribune's live results, which use Associated Press data, and the Texas Secretary of State's unofficial results show. The result is not certified. The state's official count, the canvass, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Goodwin voted twice in the House against the 2025 education savings account law, and in 2026 she pledged not to approve a budget that provides money for private schools.

The lieutenant governor is President of the Senate and, under the Senate's 2025 rules, appoints its committees and sends each bill to one of them. It also chairs the Legislative Budget Board jointly with the House speaker. But Republicans still hold the Senate majority, and the Texas Tribune reported that they can change those rules by a simple majority.

In the House she voted for the amendments that barred voucher money from the 2021 and 2023 state budgets. When Senate Bill 2, the 2025 bill that created education savings accounts for private schooling, reached the House floor, she voted no at second and third reading. Her campaign lists House Bill 3103 under a heading on resisting vouchers, but the bill concerns district contracts with out-of-state charter operators.

In a 2026 survey for the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, a teacher association, she also pledged to end state takeovers of school districts. There doesn't appear to be a public record of a pledge from her on teacher preparation or certification on her 2026 campaign pages or in her questionnaires, though she has called for more training for teachers.

On House Bill 1605 of 2023, the basis of the state-written Bluebonnet Learning materials, she voted no, then yes, then no. It is the only bill in the table below on which her votes at the reading stages went both ways.

Background and powers of the office

Her campaign biography says Goodwin moved to Austin in 1985 to attend the University of Texas and earned a master's degree in public affairs from its LBJ School in 1991. In an Amarillo Pioneer questionnaire published January 11, 2026, she described herself as a real-estate broker who owns Goodwin & Goodwin Real Estate.

She won House District 47, in western and southwestern Travis County, in 2018 and has represented it since January 8, 2019. Teach the Vote, ATPE's site for candidate information, records the same service.

In an October 15, 2026, story by Texas Public Radio, or TPR, and the Texas Tribune, she traced her interest in school money to her mother, a trustee of the Dallas Independent School District, or Dallas ISD, who "would complain that there was little local control over money".

  • Education roles. She never sat on the House Public Education or Higher Education committees. In 2025, though, she sat on the Appropriations Committee and its subcommittee on Article III, the part of the state budget that funds education. Her 2019 campaign page listed her that year on the House Democratic Caucus Special Committee on Public Education.
  • President of the Senate. Under article IV, section 16 of the Texas Constitution, the lieutenant governor "shall by virtue of his office be President of the Senate" and casts the deciding vote when the Senate is tied.
  • Committees and bill referral. The Senate's 2025 rules, for the 89th Legislature, leave committee appointments to the President: "All committees and standing subcommittees shall be appointed by the President of the Senate, unless otherwise directed by the Senate". The President also names committee chairs and "shall refer each bill to a proper committee". The rules name the Senate's education committee as the "Committee on Education K-16 (11 members)".
  • The budget. Under Government Code, section 322.001, "The lieutenant governor and the speaker are joint chairs" of the Legislative Budget Board, a permanent joint committee of the Legislature, and the lieutenant governor appoints three senators to it.
  • Limits. The Senate re-adopts its rules each session, and Republicans still hold the majority there. On November 5, 2026, the Texas Tribune reported that they "only need a simple majority to change to the rules and the authorities they give Goodwin".

Record by issue

General notes

Social media

We checked her Bluesky account, @vikkigoodwintx.bsky.social, and read it in full from November 2024 to November 9, 2026, a total of 429 original posts. All the posts below come from it.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

She pledged to end the voucher program and to approve no budget that funds private schools. In her 2026 ATPE survey on Teach the Vote, she wrote, "I will not approve a budget that provides money for private schools."

In an Amarillo Pioneer questionnaire published January 11, 2026, she listed "Increasing funding for public schools and ending the voucher program" among her top three priorities, and gave her reason: "Republicans are sending our tax dollars to private schools and as a result, are severely underfunding our neighborhood schools".

The day after the election she spoke to CBS News Texas, which published the article on November 8, 2026. "I really want to take the billion dollars that we have going into that ESA program and bring it back into our public schools", she said, and "We have a constitutional provision that we have to provide for our public schools". She did not describe a mechanism.

  • Her campaign's education page says "Vikki stood with Democrats and Republicans alike to resist voucher schemes for years" and cites her House Bill 3103 under that heading. The bill itself concerns district contracts with charter operators "not located in this state", not vouchers.
  • On religion the same page says: "Protecting Separation of Church and State – Your tax dollars shouldn't fund religious education."

Statement or interview

She has written against vouchers since 2018, and in 2025 she called for Texans to vote on them.

  • As a candidate on March 31, 2018, she wrote on her campaign blog: "Vouchers, if passed, would subtract $$ from public schools".
  • In a signed op-ed in the Austin Chronicle on October 12, 2023, she wrote: "I am strongly opposed to taking public tax dollars and spending them on private school tuition." She argued that fewer teachers would weaken the Teacher Retirement System: "we risk a systematic failure of our Teacher Retirement System".
  • The San Antonio Express-News quoted a post she made on X on April 15, 2025: "We should be putting this up for a vote of Texans. That's how we will truly know whether the people of Texas want vouchers." Governor Abbott's office replied, "This is how California is run."

Social media

  • On April 12, 2025, she posted about the House budget: "Ultimately, I couldn't vote for it with the $1 billion for vouchers."

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

She pledged to raise the basic allotment, the state's base funding per student, to simplify the funding formula and to pay educators better. Her campaign education page promises to "raise the basic allotment to previous levels, and ensure that future funding keeps up with inflation". It cites her House Bill 1770, which would set the allotment at $7,500, and promises "Better Pay for Our Educators".

Spectrum News reported one more pledge, in its own words rather than hers: that she would "commit to a 50-50 split between the state and local school districts to fund public schools".

On the formula itself, she wrote in her ATPE survey on Teach the Vote, "I plan to increase school funding and simplify the funding formula", and "Schools should have discretion on how to spend their funds". Her reason: "The current formula is overly complex, and it was made even more so in 2025."

Statement or interview

She called for more state money per student in 2018 and again in 2025. On her campaign blog in 2018 she listed recapture, the payment some districts send to the state under the school-finance system, among the causes of district cuts: "Rising property values = more $$ going to the state for other school districts". On the same blog she wrote, "I pledge to use my budgeting expertise to stop sucking funds from our FREE public schools and increase the per student funding from the state."

Her own House district includes parts of five school districts: Austin, Eanes, Lake Travis, Leander and Round Rock. Her statements on recapture, which she also calls "Robin Hood", changed between 2019 and 2025:

  • In her House newsletter of March 6, 2019, she wrote: "we can't do away with Robin Hood due to our constitution requiring an equitable education system".
  • Three months later, in her House newsletter of June 6, 2019, she wrote that House Bill 3, which she coauthored, means "all school districts in HD 47 will see a decrease in their Robin Hood recapture payments".
  • On February 11, 2025, she told FOX 7 Austin: "Honestly, if we weren't paying recapture, the state could make up that difference" and "The state isn't paying its share, in our opinion". She also supported a commission on the formula.

Social media

  • On January 23, 2025, she posted: "AISD paid $904M in recapture, or 20% of all recapture paid in Texas in 2023".
  • With House Bill 2 waiting in the Senate on May 6, 2025, she posted: "The Lt Gov has the power, but not the will."

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

She pledged less testing and an end to state takeovers of school districts. Her campaign education page says: "Less Testing, More Teaching – Our kids and teachers are drowning in STAAR test prep that steals valuable classroom time" (STAAR is the state's standardized test). On takeovers, she wrote in her ATPE survey on Teach the Vote: "I will end the state takeover of school districts and change the law so that can't happen going forward."

Statement or interview

She has opposed using tests to set teacher pay or grade schools, and she has questioned the state's replacement of school boards. In 2022 she wrote on Teach the Vote: "Standardized tests should not be used to determine teacher pay or to assign a grade to a school."

In July 2024, Spectrum News reported, she called for an investigation of Houston ISD Superintendent Mike Miles over alleged diversion of funds to a charter network. The story quoted her: "This is unconscionable, and should not be allowed".

She came back to both subjects during the 2026 campaign. A machine transcript of her September 21, 2026, podcast interview on The Texan Podcast has her saying "we spend too much time on star [STAAR] testing" and "I don't know that I support closing down schools". In the same transcript she said that the Texas Education Agency should support districts "as opposed to coming in and replacing a school board".

Social media

  • When A-F ratings were released on April 24, 2025, she posted: "Maybe it's our accountability system, or the TX Education Agency, that is failing our students?"
  • On August 27, 2025, a day after voting against House Bill 8 on second and third reading, she gave her reason: "The goal is to remove the high stakes and cut down on time spent teaching to the test. This bill won't accomplish those goals."
  • On March 6, 2026, she posted: "As Lt Governor, I will make sure the state is funding and supporting our school districts, not taking them over. We should not remove locally elected school boards."

Charter schools

Statement or interview

She criticized the growth of charter schools in 2018 and again in 2022. On her 2018 campaign blog she listed "Charter schools decrease public school enrollment" among the causes of district funding stress. Four years later she wrote on Teach the Vote that charters were meant to spread innovation, and "This has not happened, and now charters are growing at an exponential rate". She added: "I filed a bill that would provide additional transparency around new charter school locations, and I am in favor or reducing the number of charter schools".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

She made pledges on school libraries and diversity programs. In her ATPE survey on Teach the Vote, she wrote: "I will ensure librarians can do their jobs without fear of retribution."

At a panel after a film screening on book bans, which TPR and the Texas Tribune reported on October 15, 2026, she said, "Let's go back to that process that we had pre all these book ban bills". She also said she would push "to end the chilling effect and let school districts know that it's fine to have diversity and equity and inclusion", according to the same report.

Statement or interview

She has opposed state decisions on specific curriculum, the book ban bills and the Ten Commandments bill.

  • Writing on Teach the Vote in 2022, she said: "The state's role is to fund schools and to provide very broad guidance, but not to make decisions about specific curriculum and instructional materials".
  • Her 2026 answers on the same site said: "I have opposed the book ban bills since there was already a process for schools to review books when there are complaints." She added, "I also opposed bills that would limit the clubs allowed on campus."
  • During House floor debate on the Ten Commandments bill, Senate Bill 10, in May 2025, CBS News Texas quoted her: "it just seems like we're trampling over the freedom of religion by passing your bill".
  • On House Bill 1605 of 2023, which led to the state-written Bluebonnet Learning materials, she voted no at second reading on May 2, 2023, yes at third reading the next day, May 3, and no on the final version sent back from the Senate on May 17.
  • The Texas Classroom Teachers Association, or TCTA, another teacher association, reported that at the House Appropriations Committee meeting of March 31, 2025, she "had previously expressed concerns with funding for Bluebonnet Learning materials and symbolically voted against the budget as well". TCTA is our only source for her concerns about Bluebonnet.
  • Sherry Sylvester, a former Patrick adviser, said of her in October 2026, in a TPR and Texas Tribune story: "She is a knee-jerk back bencher whose votes reveal she is a fan of DEI and critical race theory and is fine with … pornography in public school libraries". The House Journal records her votes against both library bills: no on House Bill 900 in 2023 at second and third reading, and no on Senate Bill 13 in 2025 at second reading, third reading and the conference committee report.

Social media

  • On November 25, 2024, listing signs of underfunding, she posted: "Taking bible infused curriculum for $60/student".
  • Four months later, on March 26, 2025, she posted: "Public school teachers aren't the appropriate people to teach religion."

Teacher preparation and certification

Statement or interview

On teacher preparation she has called for more training, especially for teachers of students with disabilities.

  • Her campaign education page says: "Too many teachers are leaving the profession, and too few college students are choosing to go into teaching." It names the reasons as "Low pay, excessive paperwork, constant testing and safety concerns".
  • In 2022 she made the point about special education twice. Her 2022 campaign priorities included: "Provide more training to prepare our teachers to deliver the best education for our students with disabilities." And in a 2022 survey on Teach the Vote, she wrote: "For teachers who work with the population of students needing special education, I will advocate for improved and additional training."
  • A machine transcript of the September 21, 2026 podcast has her saying: "Over half of our teachers now aren't certified. So they don't have the preparation to be as effective as they can be. Maybe we need to make sure that they get the extra training that's necessary so they can handle a classroom". We did not check her figure on the uncertified share.
  • In ATPE's vote record, she voted in 2019 for House Bill 1276, on certified teachers in the early grades, and House Bill 102, on mentoring, and in 2023 against Senate Bill 798, on school counselors without teaching experience. Those votes are not in the journal records we compiled for this report.
  • Her special-education certificate bills and her coauthorship of a temporary certificate for out-of-state teachers are described under "Voting record."

Higher education

Campaign pledge

The Texas Tribune's affordability guide, republished by High Plains Public Radio, reported that she would "prioritize legislation" that "lowers college costs, including increasing community college funding and expanding college credit opportunities in high school".

Statement or interview

Her one statement on higher education concerns guns at universities. Her 2019 campaign page said her bill would "allow public universities to make the decision whether or not to allow guns on college campuses".

On November 5, 2026, in a story carried by KSAT, the Texas Tribune wrote that she and Hinojosa "campaigned on K-12 education but offered few specifics about how they would change Texas colleges and universities".

Social media

  • On October 15, 2026, she posted: "I've got a plan to make college more affordable and protect free speech for students and professors." There doesn't appear to be a plan document on her campaign site.

Other

Campaign pledge

Her campaign's issues page says "Vikki is working to expand Pre-K eligibility to include children of all public school employees", citing House Bill 494. The bill text covers the child of "a full-time employee of the school district".

In the same CBS News Texas article after the election, she said, "I want to make sure that I have conversations with each and every Senator to understand what their district needs". She named no education committee chair there, and no plan for the education savings account program.

Statement or interview

She criticized the 2023 school-safety bill's requirement of an armed person on every campus. "The potential for disastrous consequences is staggering", she said in the Texas Tribune on May 28, 2023.

She and Patrick never held a joint debate. Patrick declined, according to TPR's program The Source.

Voting record

The table lists her recorded floor votes in the Texas House, from the House Journal. The section How to read this document defines the stages.

On the four school-finance measures in the table she voted yes at every listed stage: House Bill 3 of 2019, which she coauthored, House Bill 100 of 2023, the Buckley amendment to House Bill 1 in November 2023 and House Bill 2 of 2025. She also voted for both special-education bills, Senate Bill 1716 of 2021 and Senate Bill 568 of 2025.

On vouchers she voted for both voucher-ban budget amendments and against tabling the 2023 one. In November 2023 she voted for the Raney amendment that struck the education savings account program from House Bill 1, and in 2025 she voted against Senate Bill 2 at second and third reading.

On two testing bills, House Bill 4545 of 2021 and House Bill 8 of 2025, she voted no at every listed stage, and she voted for House Bill 4 of 2025, which did not become law. She also voted no at every listed stage on ten bills on curriculum, school libraries, religion in schools, diversity programs and universities: House Bill 3979 and Senate Bill 3 of 2021; House Bill 900, Senate Bill 763, Senate Bill 17 and Senate Bill 18 of 2023; and Senate Bills 10, 12, 13 and 37 of 2025.

Five of her no votes went against most House Democrats: the 2023 budget at third reading, the 2023 school-safety bill, House Bill 3, at second and third reading, House Bill 1605 at second reading and the Buckley amendment to Senate Bill 13.

39 rows

Differences from ATPE's positions. She voted against ATPE's positions on virtual school, two 2023 teacher bills and the 2023 school-safety bill.

  • ATPE opposed the 2021 bills expanding full-time virtual school. She voted for Senate Bill 15 of 2021 on second and third reading. In 2022 she wrote on Teach the Vote that virtual school should be "a last resort".
  • ATPE also opposed House Bill 100 of 2023 over its condensed salary schedule, and Senate Bill 9 of 2023, the "Teacher Bill of Rights" with a $2,000 stipend. She voted for Senate Bill 9 on House second reading and for House Bill 100 on House third reading.
  • ATPE supported the 2023 school-safety bill, House Bill 3, and she voted against it at every stage. Her stated objection, in the Texas Tribune, was the requirement for an armed person on every campus.
  • ATPE's entry for House Bill 1605 records her as voting for it. The journal shows the three votes in the table: no, yes and no.

She explained in an April 12, 2025 post that she voted against the 2025 House budget over its voucher money. That roll call is not among the journal records we collected for this report.

Education bills she authored. None of the education bills she authored became law, as Texas Legislature Online's list of her 2025 authored bills shows.

  • She filed four bills to raise the basic allotment. House Bill 2139 of 2019 was an inflation adjustment only, and House Bill 1107 of 2023 would have set the allotment at "$6,500". In 2025 she filed House Bill 351, at "$7,160", and House Bill 1770, at "$7,500" plus an inflation index.
  • Her special-education certificate bill, House Bill 3628 of 2019, came back as House Bill 1814 in 2023. It provided that "the board shall establish a special education certificate", with the State Board for Educator Certification setting its exam and preparation-program standards. The 2019 bill cleared committee and then did not advance out of the House Calendars Committee. The 2023 bill did not advance out of committee.
  • Her charter-school bills would have set limits on charter bonds, funding and expansion. House Bill 3288 of 2019 would have required charter bonds to "be reviewed and approved by the Bond Review Board", the state board that reviews certain public bonds under Chapter 1231 of the Government Code. House Bills 2744 of 2021 and 341 of 2023, titled as funding for small and mid-sized charters, would have capped funding for larger charters and set it at "zero if the school has more than 5,000 students in average daily attendance". House Bills 438 of 2021 and 345 of 2023 would have limited charter expansion amendments to "Not more than once during each biennium".
  • In 2025 she filed House Bill 3102, which would have exempted from recapture a district whose enrollment decline is "attributable to students participating in an education savings account program", and House Bill 4104, which would have required the commissioner of education to "remove the conservator, management team, or board of managers" once a taken-over district meets set standards. House Bills 3103 and 494 are described under "Campaign pledges."
  • She coauthored House Bill 3 of 2019, which was enacted, and House Bill 4656 of 2023, to "establish a temporary teaching certificate for classroom teachers certified by other states", which was left pending in a Senate committee.

Education-oriented backers

Teacher-organization endorsements. Texas AFT, the Texas affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers, and the Texas State Teachers Association, or TSTA, both endorsed her for 2026. She thanked Texas AFT for its endorsement in a Bluesky post on January 28, 2026, and its political committee listed her among its endorsed candidates as of May 26, 2026, in a copy of its list archived June 17, 2026.

She is also on Texas AFT's November 2026 general-election list, in a copy archived October 22, 2026. TSTA endorsed her for the November 2026 general election in its 2026 list, as it had for her House seat in its 2024 list. Her campaign's organizations page shows both groups' logos.

Teacher-organization money. Six teacher-organization committees gave her direct contributions for the November 2026 general election, three of $5,000 and three of $1,000. For two of the six, the payer's report and hers give different dates.

Parent and public-school advocacy groups. In 2026 Community Voices for Public Education, a Houston group, endorsed her for the November general election, and her campaign's organizations page shows logos for two more groups: Mothers Against Greg Abbott and a "Save our schools" group that is not otherwise identified.

Parent and educator groups also backed her in earlier cycles. Teach the Vote records that Texas Parent PAC endorsed her in the 2018, 2020 and 2022 general elections, and that Texans for Public Education, a group of educators, "recommended favorably" her in 2018. The Texas Parent PAC site now lists her among candidates "supported by Texas Parent PAC when they first ran for the Texas Legislature".

Backing for her opponent. Commit to Students PAC, a Dallas committee whose purpose we did not establish, gave Dan Patrick $5,000 on August 18, 2026. The Texas Home School Coalition endorsed him.

Statewide executive offices

Nathan Johnson, attorney general-elect

Result: the Associated Press called the open seat for Johnson over Mayes Middleton, a Republican, as shown in the Texas Tribune's live results, which use Associated Press data. His margin is 631,187 votes in the Texas Secretary of State's unofficial count. The result is not certified. The state's official count, the canvass, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Johnson voted against the 2025 voucher law at both recorded Senate stages, and as a candidate he said he would not defend the Ten Commandments law.

Both laws matter to the office he won. The attorney general represents the state before the Texas Supreme Court and the courts of appeals, and two 2025 laws give the office education duties of its own. Senate Bill 2, the voucher law, has it represent the state in suits challenging the program's constitutionality or validity. Senate Bill 10, the Ten Commandments law, has it defend public schools sued over their compliance.

Johnson voted no on Senate Bill 2 at third reading in February 2025 and again in April on concurrence with the House's amendments. He voted no on Senate Bill 10 at all three recorded Senate stages. And he has opposed vouchers in every statement we found, from 2018 to 2026.

In the Texas Tribune's runoff questionnaire, he wrote that the office's duties include defending laws he dislikes but do not require arguing that an unconstitutional law is constitutional. There doesn't appear to be a public record of a pledge by him on whether he would defend the voucher law.

On teacher certification, he wrote in 2024 that he would work for a clear path to certification. A year earlier he had tried to keep the elected State Board of Education's power to reject certification rules, and his floor amendment failed, 12 to 19.

Background and powers of the office

Johnson is a Dallas trial lawyer at Thompson Coburn, and he has been the state senator for District 16 since January 2019. An October 8, 2026, Texas Tribune story recalled that he took the seat in 2018 by unseating Don Huffines. He won the attorney general runoff over Joe Jaworski on May 26, 2026, as CBS News Texas showed.

His Senate committees in 2023 and 2025 included administration, business, jurisprudence, water and agriculture, and transportation, but he never sat on the Senate education or finance committees.

The attorney general is the state's lawyer in the appeals courts. Under Government Code §402.021, the office "shall prosecute and defend all actions in which the state is interested before the supreme court and courts of appeals". Two 2025 laws add education duties to that work.

The voucher law, Senate Bill 2 or SB 2, makes the office the program's defender: "The attorney general shall represent the state in any legal action brought that challenges the constitutionality or validity of" the program. The Ten Commandments law, Senate Bill 10 or SB 10, does the same for schools: "The attorney general shall defend a public elementary or secondary school in a cause of action relating to any claims arising out of a school's compliance with this section".

Under Government Code §402.042, the office also issues legal opinions on request, including to "a regent or trustee of a state educational institution," and under Education Code §45.005 it examines school district bonds before they are issued.

The outgoing office has sued school districts. In February 2024 it sued Frisco ISD, the Frisco Independent School District, for "illegal electioneering", and in November 2025 it sued Round Rock and Leander ISDs over Ten Commandments displays.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

In the Texas Tribune's runoff questionnaire of April 23, 2026, it was Jaworski, not Johnson, who listed the voucher bill among the laws he would not defend.

Statement or interview

Every statement we found from 2018 to 2026 opposes vouchers.

  • In 2018 he listed "Block private school vouchers" among his top priorities on Teach the Vote, the candidate-information site of the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, a teacher association.
  • His Senate office's press release of October 13, 2023, said: "A private school voucher program is not fundamental to the function of the state or to the success of public education."
  • Asked by ATPE in 2024, he answered on Teach the Vote: "No. I will continue to work hard to stop the turnover of public education to the private sector."
  • Days before the Senate vote on SB 2, on January 31, 2025, he wrote in his campaign journal that "voucher programs do far more damage than good for students, parents, and education".
  • On February 5, 2025, the day of the vote, he joined a statement in the Senate Journal calling SB 2 a "voucher scam" that "siphons off billions of taxpayer dollars for private vendors".

Social media

  • Vouchers. His Senate office account posted on April 15, 2026 that "these vouchers would mainly benefit private school kids who can already afford to pay".

School funding and teacher pay

Statement or interview

He has proposed raising the basic allotment, the state's base funding per student, and tying it to inflation. His SB 233 of 2025 would have raised it "from $6,160 to $7,750 per student", in the words of an office release that his campaign reposted. In 2024 he wrote on Teach the Vote that he favored indexing the allotment to inflation, because a flat raise "would lose value over time".

In a 2019 press release on property-tax relief and school finance, his office said: "Neither can be fixed without the state fulfilling its constitutional responsibility to fund our public education system".

His 2025 newsletter said three of his bills "passed as amendments to HB 2," including free pre-kindergarten for teachers' children. House Bill 2 was a larger school finance law, and the newsletter is his own account of what went into it. It added: "The desire to have a family should not deter good people from becoming teachers or from continuing to teach".

Social media

  • The campaign account posted on January 29, 2025: "if we just funded public education at the levels set in 2019, we'd inject an extra $22 billion into the system". Three months later, on April 29, 2025, it posted: "My SB 237 provides educators parental leave after birth or adoption".

Writing about the governor's 2020 waiver of test-based promotion requirements in a campaign journal post, now archived, he said: "This reprieve from high-stakes testing will help educators give much needed attention". In 2024 he wrote on Teach the Vote that test results "should not be used to determine school accountability ratings, teacher pay increases, or student advancement to subsequent grade levels".

The article does not give the date of the interview. Asked whether the state would need private lawyers, he said, "Yes. If they want to defend unconstitutional laws". He voted yes at every listed stage on six: HB 3 of 2019 (school finance and public education overhaul), HB 3906 of 2019 (state test administration changes), SB 15 of 2021 (virtual instruction), HB 1605 of 2023 (instructional materials, the basis of Bluebonnet Learning), and HB 6 (student discipline) and HB 2 (school finance and teacher pay) of 2025.
