51 rows

On three of these votes most Senate Democrats voted the other way: both 2023 votes on HB 1605, on May 12, 2023, and the 2023 HB 3 conference report, on May 28, 2023.

The 2023 amendment on educator-certification rules. On April 6, 2023, Johnson offered an amendment to keep the State Board of Education's power to reject certification rules, and it failed, 12 to 19. SB 9, the Senate's 2023 teacher bill, would have repealed that power. His amendment, Floor Amendment 9, would "strike "(1) Section 21.042, Education Code;"" from the bill's list of repealed laws.

Section 21.042 lets the elected State Board of Education reject, but not amend, a rule of the State Board for Educator Certification by two-thirds of members present and voting. The certification board is appointed by the governor and writes the teacher-certification rules. ATPE describes the amendment as preserving the elected board's veto over certification rules.

The same day he voted for Floor Amendment 8, a $10,000 teacher raise, which also failed 12 to 19. He voted against SB 9 itself, which passed the Senate 22 to 9 but did not become law.

Other votes appear in the Senate Journal and in ATPE's record:

  • On April 17, 2019, he voted no on taking up SB 1569, a 2019 ban on electioneering by school employees with criminal penalties. After amendments, he voted yes on passage to engrossment and on final passage. ATPE opposed the bill.
  • He voted no on the Senate floor on April 16, 2025 on SB 1962 of 2025, on assessment, accountability and suits challenging the school system.
  • On SB 10 of 2025, he voted yes on the Menéndez and Eckhardt amendments to add other religious texts. They failed 10 to 20.
  • By ATPE's record, he voted for SB 798 of 2023, on ending the classroom-experience requirement for school counselors, and HB 1468 of 2021, on virtual schools, both of which ATPE opposed. We did not check the journal for these two votes.

Reports on Texas Legislature Online list the education bills he wrote. Four are listed as enacted, one of them a House bill he sponsored in the Senate, and the outcome of SB 3 of 2019, which he coauthored, was not found. His bills on the basic allotment, in 2023 and 2025, did not pass, and neither did the bill he filed in 2021, 2023 and 2025 for a state report on the cost of each new charter campus.

Statewide executive offices

Sarah Eckhardt, comptroller-elect

Result: the Associated Press called the race for Eckhardt over Don Huffines, a Republican and the appointed incumbent, as shown in the Texas Tribune's live results, which use Associated Press data. Her margin is 503,311 votes in the Texas Secretary of State's unofficial count. The result is not certified. The state's official count, the canvass, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Eckhardt voted against the 2025 education savings account law at both of its recorded Senate stages, and she has pledged to audit the program her new office runs.

Senate Bill 2 of 2025 created the accounts, which families can spend on private schooling, and put the comptroller in charge of them. The office writes the program's rules and certifies the organizations that run the accounts, but the Legislature sets the money. Even so, no budget bill passes until the comptroller certifies it.

She voted no when the Senate passed the bill at third reading in February 2025, and again in April on concurrence with the House's amendments. During the campaign, the San Antonio Express-News quoted her: "I would follow the law, but I would also follow the money vigorously". On charter schools, her 2020 platform opposed public money for charters from outside a district and said there was room for in-district ones.

She was absent, excused, for the Senate votes on two other school bills: the 2023 bill behind the Bluebonnet Learning instructional materials and the 2025 bill that replaced the state test. On teacher preparation, in 2023 she wrote a bill for grants toward computer-science teacher certification, coauthored one on accountability for educator preparation programs and voted for an amendment to keep the State Board of Education's power to reject educator-certification rules. All three failed. There doesn't appear to be a public record of her statements on teacher preparation or certification beyond those bills and votes.

Background and powers of the office

Eckhardt came to the Senate from Travis County government. Her Senate biography lists her as an assistant Travis County attorney, a county commissioner from 2006 to 2013 and Travis County judge from 2015 to 2020. Her own releases give different dates for the judgeship: one of February 13, 2025, for example, said 2014 to 2020.

She won Senate District 14 in a special election on July 14, 2020. Her committees in 2023 and 2025 included Local Government, Nominations, Veteran Affairs and Transportation, but she never sat on the Senate's education or finance committees. A December 8, 2025, Texas Tribune story covered her entry into the comptroller race that day, after a brief run for Congress.

The office she won runs the state's voucher program. Senate Bill 2 of 2025, or SB 2, created Texas Education Freedom Accounts, education savings accounts that families can spend on private schooling, and placed them under the comptroller. The bill's final, enrolled text writes the comptroller's duties into the Education Code:

  • Education Code §29.372: "The comptroller shall adopt rules and procedures as necessary to implement, administer, and enforce this subchapter".
  • Under §§29.354, 29.358 and 29.3585, the comptroller certifies the organizations that run the accounts, preapproves providers and vendors, and may suspend them.
  • §29.363: "The comptroller shall contract with a private entity to audit accounts and program participant eligibility data not less than once per year".
  • Under §§29.366, 29.371 and 29.373, the comptroller refers fraud to prosecutors and reports annually on matters including the effect on public-school capacity. The comptroller also makes decisions under the program that are "final and not subject to appeal".
  • The Legislature, not the comptroller, sets the money. Under §29.3521, the comptroller's budget request states program costs, but for each two-year budget "the amount appropriated … must be established by the legislature by appropriation for that biennium". An October 29, 2026, Texas Public Radio story put the program's cap for 2025-27 at $1 billion.

Before each regular session, the comptroller also submits a sworn revenue estimate, and under the Texas Constitution, art. III §49a, no appropriation bill passes until the comptroller endorses a certificate on it. Under Government Code §403.302, the comptroller conducts the study that determines "the total taxable value of all property in each school district". Eckhardt wrote two bills on that study, in 2021 and 2025, and neither passed.

An October 6, 2026, Texas Tribune story described reviews the acting comptroller began that fall, at Governor Abbott's request, of four independent school districts, or ISDs: Austin, Barbers Hill, El Paso and Prosper.

Record by issue

General notes

Social media

We checked her Bluesky account, @saraheckhardttx.bsky.social. It has 75 posts, from November 2024 to October 2025, and none from the 2026 campaign. Four of them concern education:

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

She pledged to audit and report on the voucher program while administering it as the law requires.

  • Her campaign site says: "The Comptroller can protect our schools & audit the voucher scheme".
  • On July 8, 2026, she told The Texan: "We need to audit the daylights out of the voucher system to show who's benefiting most, least, and not at all." Her reason: "We cannot afford to subsidize a private elite system for the five percent in private school".
  • In an October 12, 2026, written questionnaire for the Courier, she wrote that "as Comptroller my responsibility is well laid out in the law" and that she would report "which schools participate, which do not, and what parts of the state have few to no options for utilizing vouchers".
  • Two days later, on October 14, 2026, the San Antonio Express-News quoted her: "I would follow the law, but I would also follow the money vigorously".
  • In an October 29, 2026, KERA story on the Texas Public Radio site, she said of the program's budget: "You don’t haul off and double the funding right out of the gate".
  • On November 4, 2026, the day after the election, she said: "As the comptroller, my job is to vigorously follow the money and report back to the Legislature if their investment is not panning out." The Texas Tribune printed those words on November 7, 2026, and added that she "acknowledged the limitations of her office, saying that any big overhaul must come from lawmakers".

Statement or interview

She opposed the voucher law in 2025 and still opposed it after the 2026 election.

  • On February 5, 2025, the day of the Senate's third-reading vote, her office's release on SB 2 said, "Public dollars should fund public schools". That day she also joined a statement in the Senate Journal, the Senate's official record of its proceedings, calling the bill a "voucher scam".
  • Her 2026 newsletter called SB 2 a bill "which I strongly opposed".
  • After the election, Fox 26 quoted her: "This is a state subsidizing of a private industry that was doing just fine without it".

Social media

  • Vouchers. On April 24, 2025, she posted: "I spoke against SB 2 on the Senate Floor today". On May 8, 2025, she followed with: "put guardrails on Abbott’s runaway $1B voucher program".

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

School funding. In the same Texan article, she said the Rainy Day Fund, the state's reserve fund, "is so big that we could pay down the debt of every single school district that’s running a deficit". The page for a Texas Tribune event in late April 2026 quoted her second funding pledge, on the revenue estimate, the sworn estimate the comptroller submits before each regular session: she would not be "putting a political thumb on the revenue estimate at any time".

Statement or interview

School funding. She has called for full state funding of public education and for changes to recapture, the payments some districts send to the state under the school-finance system.

  • On March 22, 2023, she debated SB 4, the school property-tax cut, and the Texas Tribune quoted her that day: "If for any reason the state is unable or unwilling to pay … it will be a starvation for our public education system." The same story recorded that she voted for the bill.
  • In a 2025 release she said: "Texas must fully fund public education, increasing the basic allotment and indexing it to inflation" (the basic allotment is the state's base funding per student).
  • Her 2026 newsletter said "Austin ISD is the leader in recapture dollars sent to the State of Texas" and proposed "a discount for districts that submit recapture payments early".

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Statement or interview

She has criticized state takeovers of districts and the acting comptroller's reviews of district spending.

  • In an October 3, 2025, letter backing Austin ISD's consolidation plan, she wrote: "In Houston, it took just one school out of 273 campuses with a bad rating for the state to replace the locally elected school board with TEA appointees" (TEA is the Texas Education Agency, the state agency that oversees public schools).
  • The Beaumont Enterprise quoted her in Beaumont on August 20, 2026: "Standardized testing is a helpful tool. It’s not the only metric of educational success".
  • She called the acting comptroller's district reviews "political retribution" and "nothing more than the [comptroller] bolstering TEA's favored model of cuts, consolidations, layoffs and takeovers" in Community Impact on October 5, 2026.

Charter schools

Statement or interview

She has opposed public money for out-of-district charters. Her 2020 platform was posted after a charter-school advocacy group announced support for her unasked, and it said: "I do not support out of district charters receiving public dollars that would otherwise go to public school districts," and "I think there is room for in-district charters like Travis Heights Elementary School". The archived page names her as the speaker of the first sentence. Five years later, her 2025 letter said state law "has intentionally created an exodus to less regulated charter schools".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Statement or interview

She offered amendments to the 2023 library law and the 2025 Ten Commandments law, and all failed.

  • Her 2023 amendment to House Bill 900, or HB 900, the library-ratings law, would have required the Texas Education Agency to report "the disaggregated demographic data of" authors or main characters of rated books. It failed 12 to 19.
  • On March 18, 2025, she offered amendments to SB 10, the Ten Commandments law, that would have added or substituted a Jewish version of the text, the Five Pillars of Islam, the Seven Core Tenets of Hinduism and the Noble Eightfold Path. All failed 10 to 20.
  • In the Senate Journal she gave her reason for voting no: "This bill unconstitutionally establishes the Christian 10 Commandments as the only sanctioned text for mandatory display in Texas public schools".

Social media

  • Curriculum and religion. On March 28, 2025, posting about her amendment to SB 24 of 2025 on teaching "the horrors of communism", she wrote: "we should also include the horrors of other authoritarian ideologies". On April 15, 2025, she posted: "not one that dictates religious practices in public schools".

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

The Express-News reported that she was "particularly concerned about schools that rely on artificial intelligence for instruction and replace traditional teachers with adult guides".

Higher education

Statement or interview

During the 2023 Senate debate on SB 17, the ban on diversity, equity and inclusion offices at public universities, she said to the bill's author: "I think your bill is concerned that we've made too much progress". Three years later, the Daily Texan reported that at the LBJ School on March 2, 2026, she said the voucher program would "make it harder for public school students to get into flagship universities".

Statewide executive offices

Benjamin Flores, Land Commissioner-elect

Elected November 3, 2026, over the incumbent, Republican Dawn Buckingham. The Associated Press called the race. The returns are unofficial and not certified. The state's official count, the canvass, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Flores has pledged to protect the Permanent School Fund from voucher programs and to send more state land revenue to public schools.

The office he won has two roles tied to that fund, a state fund for public schools. The land commissioner chairs the School Land Board, which oversees the fund's lands, and holds one of nine seats on the board of the corporation that manages its investments.

Flores has held no state office, though he has sat on the Bay City City Council since 2023. His campaign Q&A pledges to protect the fund from being "raided for voucher schemes" and names raising its revenue his top priority.

Background and powers of the office

Flores works as a cybersecurity and compliance consultant and has sat on the Bay City City Council since 2023. He has held no state office.

His 2023 council-campaign site, in a copy archived May 12, 2024, said he was president of the parent association at Holy Cross Catholic School in Bay City, the private school his daughter attends.

Two accounts of his move to Bay City differ. His campaign biography says the family moved from Austin to Bay City in 2016, but his city biography says they moved to Austin in 2016 and to Bay City several years later.

The land commissioner deals with schools through the Permanent School Fund. Under Natural Resources Code §32.014, the commissioner heads the General Land Office, or GLO, and chairs the School Land Board, which oversees the fund's lands. And by Education Code §43.001, the fund includes "all income from the mineral development of permanent school fund land."

Since 2021 the fund's investments have been managed by the Texas Permanent School Fund Corporation, and Education Code §43.053 gives the land commissioner one of the nine seats on its board.

The land commissioner does not approve state guarantees of charter-school bonds. Under Education Code §45.052, the commissioner of education does.

That is the Tribune's summary of his position, not a quotation of him.

The same Q&A page names "Permanent School Fund Optimization" his top priority and says it "could generate up to $825 million more annually for Texas public schools, potentially lowering everyone's property taxes". That figure is his campaign's estimate.

His home page also pledges to expand oil, gas, wind, solar and geothermal leasing "to increase revenue benefiting the Permanent School Fund." In the League of Women Voters Houston voters guide, he wrote: "I'll responsibly lease state land for every dollar it can honestly return, publish what each acre earns, and send more of it to classrooms."

In a signed op-ed from about October 2025, he wrote that he would focus on "doing a better job funding our public schools from the state's Permanent School Fund."

Flores has never held state legislative office.

Education-oriented backers

Texas AFT COPE, the political committee of the teacher organization Texas AFT, endorsed him on its October 1, 2026, list. He had not been on its May 26 list. The Texas State Teachers Association, another teacher organization, does not list him. His campaign-finance reports to the Texas Ethics Commission through October 24, 2026, show no money from education groups.

His endorsements page lists Mothers Against Greg Abbott, a political group whose public identity is broader than schools.

For his opponent, Buckingham, the Texas Tribune guide listed the Charter Schools Now PAC, a charter-school political committee, among her endorsers, and the Texas Home School Coalition, a home-school advocacy group, endorsed her on its endorsement list.

Clayton Tucker, Agriculture Commissioner-elect

Elected November 3, 2026, over Republican Nate Sheets in an open seat. Sheets had defeated the incumbent, Sid Miller, in the Republican primary. The Associated Press called the race, and the returns are unofficial and not certified. The state's official count, the canvass, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Tucker's 2026 pledges are mostly about school meals: free meals for all children and food from Texas farmers in public schools.

The agriculture commissioner runs the Texas Department of Agriculture, which by law administers the school lunch, school breakfast and summer food service programs. Tucker's campaign meals page pledges free meals for all children and rules requiring all school food to come from Texas farmers. His October 19, 2026, newsletter put the local-food pledge differently: "I want to explore ways to connect more Texas farmers with school food programs."

He has held no public office, so he has no voting record. In 2023 the Texas Progressive Caucus, which he then led, warned Democratic lawmakers against any voucher deal. There doesn't appear to be a public record of his statements on teacher preparation beyond one line on his 2020 campaign site, in the campaign sites, interviews and posts we searched.

Background and powers of the office

Tucker has held no public office. He lost a 2020 race for Texas Senate District 24 to Dawn Buckingham and a 2021 Lampasas city-council race.

His campaign biography describes him as a rancher near Lampasas and a former kindergarten teacher in Taipei. The Texas Farmers Union, a farm organization, lists him as its current secretary on its officers page. In 2023 he was president of the Texas Progressive Caucus, a progressive political organization.

The agriculture commissioner runs the Texas Department of Agriculture, or TDA, and the department's education duties described here concern school meals. Under Agriculture Code §12.0025, TDA "shall administer" the school lunch, school breakfast and summer food service programs, among others, and section 12.0026 of the same chapter sets up a farm-to-school task force on "locally grown food products in public schools."

The school lunch program serves "more than 3 million Texas children", TDA says. Summer EBT, also called SUN Bucks, is not a TDA program: the Texas Tribune reported "a $60 million addition for the Texas Health and Human Services Commission to administer such a program."

Statewide executive offices

Jon Rosenthal, Railroad Commissioner-elect

Rosenthal was elected November 3, 2026, over Republican Bo French in an open seat. The race was called by the Associated Press. The results are unofficial and not certified. The state canvass, the official count, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Rosenthal voted against the 2025 education savings account law at both House readings, and in 2020 he wrote that he would support no voucher program.

The Railroad Commission regulates oil and gas wells and pipelines, and no statute we checked gives it authority over schools. Oil and gas production taxes do reach schools, but through the comptroller, not the commission.

His record on education comes from the Texas House. He voted no on Senate Bill 2 of 2025, which created state-funded education savings accounts for private schooling, at second and third reading. On House Bill 2 of 2025, on school finance and teacher pay, he voted yes at second and third reading, then no on the final version.

In a 2020 survey he called the state's standardized tests "detrimental to the point of being criminal". In 2025 he voted against House Bill 8, the testing law that replaced them, at all three recorded stages. There doesn't appear to be a public record of his reasons for these votes or for his vote against the final version of House Bill 2.

His work on teacher preparation and certification is in bills, chiefly one he filed in four sessions, first in 2019, on assigning students to uncertified teachers.

Background and powers of the office

Rosenthal has represented Texas House District 135, in northwest Harris County, since January 2019. He first won the seat in 2018 over the Republican incumbent, Gary Elkins, as his campaign site and Community Impact both say.

A Texas Public Radio story described him as a mechanical engineer with 25 years in oil and gas who did not seek re-election to the House in order to run for the Railroad Commission.

His House committees in 2019, 2021, 2023 and 2025 included Energy Resources, County Affairs, and Agriculture and Livestock. He never sat on the House Public Education or Higher Education committees.

The Railroad Commission of Texas regulates oil and gas wells and pipelines, under Natural Resources Code §81.051. The production taxes on that oil and gas reach schools through the comptroller, not the commission, under Tax Code §202.353 and §201.404. After other deductions, the comptroller deposits "one-fourth of the revenue collected from the tax imposed by this chapter to the credit of the foundation school fund", a state fund for public schools.

Record by issue

General notes

Campaign pledge

His 2020 pledges are his written answers to a survey by the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, a teacher association that does not endorse candidates. ATPE published them on its Teach the Vote site. He did not answer the association's 2022 or 2024 surveys.

Social media

We searched all 121 original posts on his Bluesky account, jon-rosenthaltx.bsky.social. In one, on July 27, 2026, he wrote that "my opponent is attacking Texas seniors, students, and neighbors with disabilities". The post states no education policy.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

Private-school vouchers and education savings accounts. Asked in the 2020 survey whether he would support any voucher, education savings account or tax-credit program, he answered: "No. Nope. No way." An education savings account is a state-funded account that parents can spend on private schooling. Five years later he voted against Senate Bill 2, the law that created them in Texas.

Statement or interview

Private-school vouchers and education savings accounts. He spoke against vouchers in 2023 and again in 2025. On October 12, 2023, he said, as quoted by the Houston Chronicle: "Vouchers are a scam that take money out of our schools." The Chronicle also reported his view that the money "would be better used to increase the basic allotment and give raises to teachers" (the basic allotment is the base per-student amount in the state formula).

On April 2, 2025, he told the Houston Chronicle of Senate Bill 2 of 2025, the bill creating education savings accounts: "It's not a school choice package at all, it's a discount for kids who are already in private schools." On April 17 he voted against the bill at second and third reading.

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

On election night in 2018 he told Community Impact: "We're going to address education first and health care second."

Two years later, in the 2020 survey, he wrote of the teacher retirement system, "Keep the defined benefit pension plan for sure," and of pay: "Teacher pay should be determined on multiple criteria (certainly including seniority!)."

Statement or interview

He asked for more state money for schools and for raises for educators in 2019, and for more school funding again in 2024.

  • Community Impact reported on June 26, 2019, that "he would like to see more comprehensive school system funding to provide more raises to educators."
  • The Houston Chronicle reported that on May 6, 2024, he spoke on budget and librarian cuts at a board meeting of the Cypress-Fairbanks Independent School District, or Cypress-Fairbanks ISD. The paper wrote that he was "asking every Texan watching to call their representatives and ask for increased funding to public education."
  • In the same story, the Chronicle wrote that he was one of six area House members who signed a letter "urging the Texas Education Agency to release the $30 million from the TEA's surplus". Republican Rep. Tom Oliverson led that bipartisan group.
  • On May 13, 2024, a week after the board meeting, he and about 40 lawmakers asked Gov. Greg Abbott for a special session. Their letter, as Spectrum News printed it, said: "These issues arise from the state's failure to improve school funding since 2019". Abbott replied that the signers had voted against a school-funding bill tied to vouchers, according to ABC13.

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

The same survey set out his case against the state tests. He called STAAR, the state's standardized tests, "detrimental to the point of being criminal" and set a goal to "repeal and replace" them. He wrote where he would begin: "First steps are to decouple it from school accountability and also further increase pilot programs for alternative testing and evaluation systems." For low-rated schools he wrote: "How about instead we allocate EXTRA resources to struggling schools".

Statement or interview

On August 13, 2025, he told the Houston Press, "I'm an anti-STAAR crusader," and said he wanted to "revise or actually kill the STAAR test."

Charter schools

Campaign pledge

In the same survey he wrote that "not all charter operations are inherently evil" but that "With today's current budget crunch there is NO WAY that any new charters should be approved."

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Statement or interview

After the Cypress-Fairbanks ISD board removed science-textbook chapters on vaccines, climate change and cultural diversity, he said on June 17, 2024, in the Houston Chronicle: "As a science-based career professional and a state rep who values and supports public education I'm appalled".

Higher education

Campaign pledge

On his 2026 campaign priority page he pledges to "partner with local business and community colleges on paid training."

Statement or interview

On May 22, 2023, during House debate on Senate Bill 18, the 2023 bill on faculty tenure, he said: "My family came to Texas because of the tenure program at The University of Texas." He voted against the bill that day and again at third reading on May 23.

Other

Statement or interview

Other: oil and gas revenue. On July 26, 2026, he told KTAB: "The revenues that come from oil and gas production pay for our schools, our roads, our parks, and so much more."

The note "most House Democrats voted the other way" marks the 11 votes on which a majority of House Democrats on the journal roll voted differently from him.

Six of his votes in the table concern the voucher-ban budget amendments, the amendment striking the education savings account program, or Senate Bill 2, and each went against vouchers. He voted for the budget amendments barring voucher money in 2021 and 2023 and against the motion to table the 2023 one, for the 2023 amendment that struck the education savings account program from the school-finance bill, and against Senate Bill 2 at both readings in 2025.

65 rows

How a teacher association describes some of these votes. ATPE's profile lists several of his votes that went against the association's positions. According to ATPE's Teach the Vote profile, he voted for two 2021 bills expanding full-time virtual schools, House Bill 1468 and Senate Bill 15, which ATPE opposed.

ATPE records that he voted against the 2023 school-safety conference report and the 2025 discipline bill, House Bill 6, which ATPE supported. And he voted for Senate Bill 9 of 2023, which ATPE opposed "as insufficient in terms of providing a meaningful increase in educator compensation", in the words of Teach the Vote.

ATPE also reports a vote on House Bill 547 of 2021, on home-schooled students' participation in public-school activities. He was recorded as voting yes on concurrence but entered a statement that he intended to vote no, ATPE says. The table shows the same thing on Senate Bill 569 in 2025: recorded yes at second reading, with a statement that he intended to vote no.

Bills he authored on education.

  • Teacher preparation and certification. In four sessions he filed the same bill on assigning students to uncertified teachers: House Bill 1276, or HB 1276, in 2019, then HB 800 in 2021, HB 1005 in 2023 and HB 362 in 2025. The 2019 text said that in districts of at least 5,000 students, a student in grades 1 to 6 "may not be assigned for two consecutive school years to a teacher who" has less than one year of experience and lacks the required certificate. Parents could consent to such an assignment. The 2019 bill passed the House on April 25, 2019, and did not pass the Senate, according to Teach the Vote. He was also a joint author of HB 116 of 2019, on educator training, and a coauthor of HB 1569 of 2023, on training computer-science teachers.
  • Testing, accountability and state takeovers. His bills would have changed how the state takes over school districts and how state tests count in school ratings. HB 3545 of 2019 would have replaced a state-appointed board of managers with a "community management board" including "a classroom teacher from the school district or campus." HB 3071 of 2021, filed with Rep. Garnet Coleman, said "the commissioner may not order the appointment of a board of managers to govern a school district unless at least 15 percent of the campuses" were rated unacceptable. HB 2661 of 2023 would have ended the use of state tests as indicators of achievement in school ratings.
  • Charter schools. HB 1320 of 2021, which he refiled in 2023 and 2025, would have applied state travel-expense rules to charter schools spending state money. It never passed.
  • School funding and teacher pay. HB 3380 of 2025 would have raised the basic allotment from $6,160 to "the lesser of $7,500" or a formula amount, with an inflation adjustment. He was a coauthor of HB 3 of 2019, the school-finance law.
  • Higher education. HB 626 of 2021, which became law, expanded an adult career-education grant program.

Education-oriented backers

  • Texas AFT COPE, the political committee of Texas AFT (the Texas affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers), endorsed him on its May 26 and October 1, 2026 lists. He is not on the 2026 list of the Texas State Teachers Association, or TSTA.
  • In his earlier House races he had backing from education groups. TSTA's 2024 list includes him, and its political committee gave him $500 on November 18, 2024, after that general election. In 2018, in Community Impact, he credited "backing from the Cy-Fair branch of the American Federation of Teachers". And Teach the Vote lists him as "Endorsed in the 2022 general election by Texas Parent PAC," a parent political committee.
  • The Texas Home School Coalition endorsed his opponent, French, on its endorsement list.

Texas Legislature

The Texas Legislature after the 2026 election

Democrats are projected to control the Texas House and Republicans the Texas Senate, so neither party will hold both chambers of the Legislature. As of November 9, 2026, the MultiState tracker counted 81 Democrats and 64 Republicans in the 150-member House, with five seats last held by Republicans not yet called. If current leads hold, the House will have 83 Democrats and 67 Republicans.

The 31-member Senate is projected at 19 Republicans to 12 Democrats. The Texas Tribune reported that count on November 5, 2026, and Dan Patrick, the outgoing lieutenant governor, gave the same count on November 9, according to Texas Public Radio. The Texan reported that Republicans hold 20 seats. No legislative result is certified, and the state canvass, the official count, ends by December 7, 2026.

The Legislature writes the state's education laws and its two-year budget, and the Senate also confirms the governor's appointees, including the commissioner of education, whose appointment needs the Senate's consent under §7.051 of the Education Code.

The 2027 regular session opens on January 12, 2027, under Government Code §301.001. The constitution limits it to 140 days, so its last day is May 31, 2027. Hinojosa takes office as governor a week after the session opens, on January 19, 2027, under article IV, section 4 of the constitution, and FOX 26 gave the same date. Bills can be filed before then: the Texas Municipal League reported that legislators and legislators-elect can file them from November 9, 2026, until March 12, 2027.

The table shows the votes each action takes and whether either party can take it alone on projected results. In the Senate, the regular order of business is the procedure for taking up bills, and setting it aside to take up a bill takes five-ninths of those present.

ActionRuleVotes neededWho can do it alone
House: pass a billmajority (Texas Tribune)a majority of those voting, 76 if all 150 voteDemocrats
House: elect a Speakermajority (Texas Tribune)a majority of those voting, 76 if all 150 voteDemocrats
Senate: take up a bill out of the regular order of businessfive-ninths of those present (Senate vote chart)18 of 31Republicans
Senate: change the Senate's rulesmajority of all members (Senate Rules)16 of 31Republicans
Senate: confirm an appointeetwo-thirds of those present (constitution)21 of 31neither party
Override a vetotwo-thirds of the members present in the chamber where the bill began, then two-thirds of the members of the other chamber (constitution, article IV, section 14)100 in the House and 21 in the Senate when all attendneither party
Quorum to do business"Two-thirds of each House shall constitute a quorum to do business" (constitution, article III, section 10)100 of 150 in the House and 21 of 31 in the Senateneither party

Because of the quorum rule in the constitution, the minority party in either chamber can stop business by staying away. For a veto override, the constitution requires that "two-thirds of the members present agree to pass the bill" in the first chamber, and in the second the bill must be "approved by two-thirds of the members of that House". The Legislature has not done so since 1979, when it overrode a veto on a bill under Governor William P. Clements Jr.

Two Senate seats will also be empty for a time. Sarah Eckhardt's and Nathan Johnson's seats become vacant when they take statewide office and stay vacant until special elections, which the Austin American-Statesman reported had not been called. Until then, confirmation would take 20 of 29 senators if all attend.

The lieutenant governor presides over the Senate and, under the Senate's rules, appoints its committees and refers its bills. The Senate adopts those rules at the start of the session, which opens January 12, 2027, and a majority of 16 senators can take those powers away. The lieutenant governor's deciding vote in a tie comes from the constitution and cannot be removed that way.

Patrick urged Republican senators on November 9 to take those powers from his successor, Vikki Goodwin. The Statesman reported that Republican senators had been meeting privately to discuss it, but no resolution has been filed. There doesn't appear to be a public record of a sitting Republican senator backing a specific change, and Senator Paul Bettencourt, a Republican, said the decision was up to the Senate, the Dallas Morning News reported. The Statesman quoted Goodwin as hoping for "a collaborative environment in the Senate."

Earlier cases differ. North Carolina's Democrat-controlled Senate took such powers from the lieutenant governor in 1989. The Texas Senate did not in 1997 and 1998, when its majority and Lieutenant Governor Bob Bullock, a Democrat, were of different parties, the Statesman reported. Our estimate of this change is in the sections "Implications for the future" and "How we made the estimates", the only parts of this document that look ahead.

In the House, the Speaker presides and appoints committee chairs, and the members elect the Speaker by a majority on January 12, 2027. Senfronia Thompson, a Houston Democrat, is the leading candidate. The Texas Tribune reported that Eddie Morales Jr. withdrew and endorsed her on November 6, and that she released a list of 90 supporters, eight of them Republicans. She said she would appoint members of both parties to chair committees, the same article reported. The Republican caucus has not chosen a nominee.

U.S. Senate

James Talarico, U.S. senator-elect

Result: the Associated Press called the race for Talarico over Ken Paxton, a Republican, as shown in the Texas Tribune's live results, which use Associated Press data. His margin is 1,195,609 votes in the Texas Secretary of State's unofficial count. The result is not certified. The state's official count, the canvass, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Talarico sat on the House Public Education Committee from 2019 through 2025, and he voted against the 2025 education savings account law in committee and on the House floor.

In the Senate his education powers are federal. Senators vote on the appropriations that fund the U.S. Department of Education and confirm its Secretary, but the office has no direct authority over Texas teacher certification or state school-finance formulas.

The law in question, Senate Bill 2 of 2025, created state-funded education savings accounts that families can spend on private schooling. He voted no on it in committee, then again at second and third reading. Every statement we found from him between 2023 and 2026 opposed vouchers. In 2022 he also wrote that high-quality nonprofit public charter schools have a role in the education system.

He has said he once had 45 students in one classroom, and that account is disputed. The Daily Wire reported, citing a New York Times profile, that his largest class had 30 students. His campaign answered in the same article that 45 students were placed in his classroom before they were redistributed.

His one pledge on educator preparation is to expand federal programs such as the Teacher Quality Partnership.

Background and powers of the office

A January 16, 2026, Texas Tribune article laid out his years in the classroom. He taught sixth-grade language arts at Rhodes Middle School in San Antonio ISD (independent school district) from 2011 to 2013 as a Teach For America corps member, and then spent a year at the Harvard Graduate School of Education.

By 2016 he was Central Texas executive director of Reasoning Mind, a nonprofit offering computer-based math instruction, the title the San Antonio Report gave him. On November 6, 2018, he won a special election to the Texas House.

His page on Teach the Vote lists him as the member for House District 52 and then, after his 2022 reelection, for District 50. The site belongs to the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, a teacher association that does not endorse candidates. From 2019 to 2025 he also worked for Maya Consulting LLC, an education consulting firm, and his Senate financial disclosure lists $83,333.40 that the firm paid him in 2025.

In the House he sat on the Public Education Committee in all four regular sessions from 2019 through 2025. His member page adds four more assignments. In 2023 he also sat on the select committee that took up vouchers and on two House-Senate conference committees, one on school chaplains, Senate Bill 763 (SB 763), and one on pre-kindergarten teacher requirements, House Bill 2729 (HB 2729). In 2025 he was vice chair of a Public Education subcommittee on academic and career education.

A senator's education powers are federal. Senators vote on the appropriations that fund the U.S. Department of Education, and the U.S. Constitution says "No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law". They also give "Advice and Consent" on officers of the United States, among them the Secretary of Education. But the office has no direct authority over Texas teacher certification, state school-finance formulas or the Texas Education Agency, the state agency that oversees public schools.

Record by issue

General notes

Campaign pledge

Unless another source is named, the pledges below are on his campaign's public-education page, which was published January 2, 2026, and modified October 12, 2026.

Statement or interview

Quotations are his own words unless marked as campaign or reporter text.

Social media

The posts below are all from X. We read his account there, @jamestalarico, through posts embedded on his campaign pages and through Thread Reader, and we did not read his other accounts.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

Two of his campaign pages pledge to oppose vouchers. The public-education page pledges to "Reject the voucher scams being pushed by billionaire mega-donors that defund public schools to subsidize private education for the wealthiest Americans". The rural-investment page pledges to "Oppose the federal voucher scam being pushed by billionaires like Betsy DeVos," though it names no federal bill.

Statement or interview

Every statement we found from him between 2023 and 2026 opposed private-school vouchers.

  • On April 7, 2023, after the House barred state budget money for vouchers, his office issued a release, which the Gilmer Mirror reprinted: "They have a simple strategy: First, demonize, and then dismantle public education".
  • At the House select committee's hearing in July 2023, as reported by ATPE, he said: "It’s my opinion we shouldn’t be messing with any pet projects or education savings accounts until we do the $1,000 increase." He also asked the Texas Education Agency what federal protections special-education students give up by taking an education savings account, the state-funded account parents can spend on private schooling.
  • He answered his 2024 ATPE candidate survey on Teach the Vote this way: "No. I am against voucher scams in any shape or size and will never vote to defund our public schools".
  • When the House debated SB 2, the bill that created the state's education savings accounts, on April 16, 2025, he said: "This amendment would send this private school voucher bill to the voters of Texas for their approval before it can be implemented." His reason was that "private schools can deny admission to any kid for any reason they want." The House tabled the amendment.
  • The Texas Tribune quoted him at a primary debate on January 24, 2026: "I have gone toe to toe with the billionaires who are trying to dismantle public education in this state".

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

He has called for full funding of the Department of Education and a raise for educators. At a CNN town hall on October 14, 2026, he said, "One, I would make sure that we fully fund the Department of Education." He also said: "I think we can do so much to finally pass a pay raise for our hardworking educators." He named no federal mechanism for the raise.

Earlier, KLTV reported on May 29, 2026 that "he hopes to push at the federal level to incentivize states to get teachers above the national average".

Statement or interview

School funding, teacher pay and class size. He voted for the 2025 school-finance law while calling it inadequate, and he has said that an education system built on property wealth is unequal. The law was HB 2, on school finance and teacher pay, and on April 16, 2025, he said on the House floor: "I voted for that bill in committee and on the floor, but I also made the point on this back microphone that it was inadequate to the crisis that our schools are facing".

Explaining why he left teaching, he told the Tribune: "An education system that is built on property wealth is always going to be inherently unequal". At the CNN town hall, he said: "I believe that educators should be sitting at the decision-making table when it comes to making decisions about education policy".

His campaign's public-education page says he "Overhauled Texas’s school finance system and invested over $6.5 billion into public schools for teacher pay raises, educator training, new literacy and math proficiency initiatives". That was the 2019 law, HB 3, and in 2024 he wrote on Teach the Vote that "crafting HB 3 and fixing our broken school finance system, was my top priority". The law's bill history lists him as one of about 140 coauthors, not one of its five authors.

The size of his class is in dispute. On his campaign page and at the CNN town hall he has said, "At one point, I had 45 students in one classroom".

On October 28, 2026, the Daily Wire, a conservative outlet, reported, citing a New York Times profile, that "Texas Education Agency documents reviewed by the Times, however, indicate that the largest class period he taught at Rhodes Middle School had 30 students, while most of his classes ranged from 22 to 27". We could not open the Times profile, so the class-size figure is reported here secondhand. The same article quoted the campaign spokesman, JT Ennis: "After having 45 students placed in his classroom, James worked with school administrators to redistribute students across classes and create the learning environment that his students deserved".

Social media

  • On May 14, 2021, he posted: "I just passed legislation to limit the size of pre-k classes to 22 students in Texas". On January 24, 2023, he wrote: "Today I’m introducing legislation to give every teacher in Texas a $15,000 pay raise".

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

Testing and instruction. The public-education page has one pledge on this, for grants "to encourage public schools to adopt evidence-based strategies like phonics, early literacy programs, and 1:1 intensive tutoring".

Statement or interview

In his 2022 and 2024 surveys on Teach the Vote, he wrote that tests should not be "the sole, or even the majority, means of evaluating teachers", and that "the current testing regime represents an overcorrection and must be addressed".

On July 13, 2026, in Texas Metro News, he spoke about the state takeover of Houston ISD and about vouchers: "There is a coordinated effort by some of the most powerful politicians, and some of the wealthiest mega donors to dismantle public education".

Charter schools

Statement or interview

He supports nonprofit public charters as a form of public-school choice. "I believe there is a role for high-quality nonprofit public charter schools in our education system," he wrote on Teach the Vote in 2022, adding that his concern was "not with the number of public charter schools, but with the quality".

He came back to charters on the House floor on April 16, 2025: "we could open more magnets, more academies, more career and technical schools, more public charter schools, eliminate the wait-lists". He also said: "I'm talking about real school choice, which I support and have supported since I got to this body".

Seth Rau, who wrote Talarico's 2018 education platform, wrote in SCHOOLED on March 10, 2026 that he "has been very close to the leaders of the Texas charter school movement, and they hosted many of his earliest fundraisers during his 2018 campaign".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Curriculum and religion in schools. His freedom-family-faith page pledges to "reject policies that force religion into neutral public spaces like schools, prisons, courts, and the military".

Statement or interview

He opposed the bills on race in the curriculum and on the Ten Commandments, offered amendments to the school chaplains bill, and questioned Commissioner Mike Morath about Bluebonnet Learning.

  • On May 28, 2021, speaking on HB 3979, the 2021 bill limiting how teachers address race, he asked: "Is it fair to say that any bill that strikes language condemning racism is a racist bill?" A Texas Tribune article carried by Click2Houston printed the question, and an ATPE blog post recorded that his point of order against the Senate's amendments was sustained.
  • SB 1515, a Senate bill requiring Ten Commandments displays, came to a committee hearing on May 2, 2023. He said there, in remarks carried by KUTV: "This bill to me is not only unconstitutional, it's not only un-American, I think it is also deeply un-Christian".
  • On May 8, 2023, the House adopted his amendment to SB 763, the school chaplains bill, requiring chaplains to be endorsed by an organization the Department of Defense recognizes. His second amendment, requiring parental consent before a child meets a chaplain, failed 61 to 76.
  • In 2024 he asked Morath about Bluebonnet Learning, the state-written materials that HB 1605 of 2023 led to: "How do you believe teachers will respond to elementary school students when they ask how a human being can rise from the dead?" The 74 printed the question.
  • In 2025, on SB 10, the Ten Commandments law, he said: "I worry that these kinds of bills will actually create a new generation of atheists who think our religion is more about power than love." The Austin Chronicle placed this in an April debate with Rep. Candy Noble. Texas Public Radio described a similar argument in the May 24, 2025, floor debate, where he said, "The separation of church and state doesn't just protect the state. It also protects the church".

Social media

  • Curriculum and religion. On HB 3979 he posted, on May 28, 2021: "If kids are old enough to experience racism, then they're old enough to learn about it", in a thread on Thread Reader. On May 3, 2023, he posted: "This bill is not only un-constitutional and un-American, it’s deeply un-Christian". A March 1, 2024, post embedded on his faith page said: "The 25 largest school districts in Texas all rejected replacing counselors with chaplains". A May 29, 2025, post embedded on the same page said: "forcing teachers to post the Ten Commandments violates the most important commandment: love thy neighbor".

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

His one pledge on educator preparation, on the public-education page, reads: "Hire more teachers and equip them with what they need to succeed: Expand programs like the Teacher Quality Partnership, the Supporting Effective Educator Development program, and the TEACH grant that fund and enhance teacher training and are helping to close the teacher workforce gap". It gives no dollar amounts and does not mention residencies or alternative certification.

Statement or interview

He entered teaching through Teach For America after graduating from the University of Texas. The sources differ on the year he graduated: 2011 according to the Daily Texan, 2010 according to the Texas Tribune, which gave his teaching years as 2011 to 2013.

  • On the supply of certified teachers, his 2024 survey answer on Teach the Vote said "the best way to have adequate numbers of trained and certified teachers is to listen to Governor Abbott's own Teacher Vacancy Task Force which recommended increasing teacher pay." He also named retirement benefits and workload. The answer is about pay, not about preparation or certification routes.
  • The House Public Education Committee held an interim hearing on teacher certification on August 13, 2024. The Texas Classroom Teachers Association, or TCTA, a teacher association, reported that he "asked for more details about the survey", meaning TCTA's member survey on uncertified teachers, and TCTA named him among members "particularly supportive of teachers and the teaching profession throughout the hearing."
  • A machine transcript of the Joe Rogan podcast of July 18, 2025, on Rosetta, has him saying high-poverty schools give "the kids who have the most troubles to the first year teachers … Almost like a hazing thing".
  • Under "Voting record" are his two educator-workforce bills: the 2021 law that changed the composition of the State Board for Educator Certification, which sets certification rules, and a 2025 bill on teachers' appeals under the state's teacher-designation pay system. His votes on certification and counselor bills are there too.
  • Rep. Carl Tepper, a Republican, said in the Texas Tribune that he "should never claim to be an expert in education because of two years in the classroom".

Higher education

Campaign pledge

His pledges here are on career programs and federal student aid. The public-education page pledges to improve "junior college and Career and Technical Education programs".

His positions on student aid come through two news accounts. A Texas Tribune article carried by KSAT on October 8, 2026 said he "has called for a reversal of federal cuts to the U.S Department of Education and for additional funding for Pell Grants and other student aid". On October 21, 2026, FOX 7 Austin, drawing on the campaign and his legislative remarks, wrote that he "advocated for expanding the value of federal Pell Grants, indexing them to inflation" and "supports student debt relief".

Statement or interview

He voted against SB 17 of 2023 and SB 37 of 2025, the laws on university diversity offices and university governance, at second reading, third reading and the conference report. The votes are under "Voting record."

Other

Campaign pledge

The public-education page also pledges universal pre-kindergarten "for every 3- and 4-year-old" and protection of "federal oversight that ensures special education students receive the funding and support they need". It pledges, too, an expansion of "the National School Lunch and School Breakfast programs," more school counselors, and federal guidelines "that can help states and schools safely use AI in the classroom".

Statement or interview

On Teach the Vote he called HB 3 of 2023, which required an armed security officer at each campus, "another unfunded mandate on public schools".

On September 9, 2026, he said, "I will oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it risks safety or fairness." The Texas Tribune's headline called this a reversal. In 2021 he had voted against HB 25, which limited school sports teams by biological sex.

His campaign page and a 2023 post on X say he put Narcan, a drug that reverses opioid overdoses, "on EVERY school campus". The enrolled text of the law he sponsored, SB 629 of 2023, requires an opioid-antagonist policy "at each campus in the district that serves students in grades 6 through 12".

Social media

  • On May 26, 2023, he posted: "I just passed a bill to put Narcan on EVERY school campus in Texas".

Voting record

The House Journal records his House floor votes in the table below. Each is a vote on the bill at the stage named, not on any single provision.

Of the 60 votes in the table, he cast 28 yes and 31 no, and he was absent, excused, for one. On every voucher vote in the table, he took the side against vouchers. He voted for the budget amendments barring state money for vouchers in 2021 and 2023, against the motion to table the 2023 amendment, and for striking the education savings account article from House Bill 1 of the fourth special session in November 2023. In 2025 he voted against SB 2 at second and third reading.

He voted yes at every listed stage of three school-finance bills: HB 3 of 2019, HB 100 of 2023 and HB 2 of 2025. On nine bills about curriculum, library books, school chaplains, the Ten Commandments, diversity, equity and inclusion programs, parental rights and university governance, he voted no at every stage at which he cast a vote on the bill itself: HB 3979 and SB 3 of 2021; HB 900, SB 763 and SB 17 of 2023; and SB 10, SB 12, SB 13 and SB 37 of 2025. He also voted no on SB 1716 of 2021, on supplemental special-education services and instructional materials accounts, at third reading.

On testing, he voted for HB 4 of the 2025 regular session, which did not become law, at second and third reading, and against HB 8 of the 2025 second special session, which replaced the state test, at second reading, third reading and concurrence in Senate amendments. Two bills had his yes vote at second and third reading and his no vote at the last stage: HB 1605 of 2023, the instructional-materials bill behind Bluebonnet Learning, at concurrence, and HB 3 of 2023, the school-safety bill, at the conference report. He had coauthored HB 3 of 2023 and voted against its final version.

On two bills his committee vote was the opposite of every floor vote he cast. He voted no on HB 4545 in committee on April 15, 2021 and yes at each floor stage, and he voted yes on SB 1716 in committee on May 18, 2021, and no at third reading on May 26, 2021. The committee voted on SB 1365 three times, on May 7, 2021, again on May 7, 2021 and on May 23, 2021, and the minutes do not say why. He voted no the first two times and yes the third.

ATPE's candidate profile records six more House votes, which we did not check against the House Journal. He voted yes on five of them and no on SB 798 of 2023, which ended the requirement that school counselors have classroom-teaching experience.

ATPE opposed the bills on property-tax exemptions for charter schools, virtual schools and home-schooled students in public-school activities, and he voted for all three. ATPE also opposed SB 15 of 2021, on virtual instruction, which he voted for as well. He explained that vote on Teach the Vote in 2022: "I supported SB 15 because the funding it provides is necessary during such a challenging time for students and teachers." Teach the Vote also shows that ATPE supported HB 3 of 2023, whose final version he voted against, and was neutral with concerns on HB 8 of 2025, which he voted against.

Education-oriented backers

Teacher-organization endorsements. Two teacher organizations endorsed him for the general election. Texas AFT COPE, the political committee of Texas AFT, the Texas affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers, endorsed him on March 13, 2026, after the primary, and said he "has worked tirelessly against the voucher scam". The committee's general-election list still named him in a copy captured October 22, 2026.

The Texas State Teachers Association, or TSTA, a statewide teacher association, lists him on its general-election list, and on October 13, 2026, it called him "Our endorsed candidate for US Senate" in a news post. Its primary list had no Senate entry.

Teacher-organization money. Two national teacher-union committees each gave $5,000 to his Senate campaign. The 16 earlier contributions in the table, from four Texas committees between 2018 and 2025, went to his Texas House campaigns. One of the four is ATPE's committee, which says on its PAC page that its contributions "do not constitute a public endorsement by ATPE".

Texas Supreme Court

The Texas Supreme Court and public schools

The four Democratic wins in 2026 "will leave the GOP with a 5-4 advantage on the Supreme Court," the Texas Tribune wrote on November 4, 2026, with Maggie Ellis as chief justice. Before the election, "All of the current justices are Republicans," the Tribune's guide to the races said.

The Texas Supreme Court is the state's highest court for civil cases, and its justices "get to decide which cases to review, and their rulings … are final," the same guide explained.

School cases reach the court from the intermediate courts of appeals, the appeals courts that sit below it. The dockets cited in this section show these kinds of school cases:

  • suits against the Texas Education Agency, the commissioner of education and the State Board for Educator Certification, which licenses and disciplines educators
  • state takeovers of districts
  • teacher contracts and pay grievances
  • school finance
  • immunity defenses of districts and charter schools

Until 2024, most suits against state agencies went on appeal to the Third Court of Appeals in Austin, where Ellis, Chari Kelly and Gisela Triana sit. Senate Bill 1045 of 2023 changed that. It created a Fifteenth Court of Appeals with "exclusive intermediate appellate jurisdiction" over cases brought by or against state agencies.

The law applies to appeals perfected on or after September 1, 2024. On that date it moved to the new court the pending cases of that kind in other courts of appeals that had been filed on or after September 1, 2023. Cases filed earlier stayed in the Third Court.

There doesn't appear to be a public record of statements by any of the four winners on vouchers, school finance, testing or the state takeover of the Houston Independent School District. The rules for judges limit what candidates for the court may say. Canon 5(1) of the Code of Judicial Conduct says: "A judge or judicial candidate shall not: (i) make pledges or promises of conduct in office regarding pending or impending cases, specific classes of cases, specific classes of litigants, or specific propositions of law that would suggest to a reasonable person that the judge is predisposed to a probable decision in cases within the scope of the pledge." Canon 3B(10) applies a similar limit on public comment about pending cases to candidates.

As of November 9, 2026, these education cases were pending at the court or could reach it. Two had been argued and were undecided.

  • Morath v. Texas State Teachers Association, No. 25-0527. The case challenges the commissioner's rule for district campuses run by outside partners under Senate Bill 1882 of 2017. The court granted review on June 12, 2026, heard argument on October 7, 2026, and has not ruled. Ellis joined the Third Court opinion under review.
  • Texas Public Policy Foundation v. Highland Park ISD, No. 25-0759. The question is whether an exception in the Public Information Act, the state law that requires government bodies to disclose information on request, covers attorney-client material, here a school district's investigation report. The court heard argument on October 8, 2026, and has not ruled.
  • Harris County Department of Education Public Facility Corp. v. Paradigm Construction, No. 26-0790. This dispute over a construction contract comes from Kristen Hawkins's district court and concerns governmental immunity, the rule that protects government bodies from some lawsuits. The case is at the petition stage. The court ordered a response by November 2, 2026, and on October 14, 2026, it granted in part a motion to extend that deadline and set the response as due December 2, 2026.
  • Excellence 2000 Inc. v. Texas Education Agency, No. 26-1213. The petition was filed October 22, 2026, and is under review. We did not read its subject.
  • In re Midland ISD, No. 26-0867. On August 12, 2026, the court denied an emergency mandamus petition that the Midland school district brought against the commissioner of education. A mandamus petition asks a higher court to order an official or a lower court to act or to undo an act.
  • School ratings. Two suits over A-F ratings, the state's letter grades for districts and schools, the Kingsville ISD and Pecos-Barstow-Toyah ISD cases, ended in the Fifteenth Court of Appeals in 2025. There doesn't appear to be a Supreme Court petition in either.
  • There doesn't appear to be a Texas Supreme Court case on the 2025 Ten Commandments law, which requires the Ten Commandments to be displayed in classrooms, or on the 2025 education savings account law, the state's voucher program.

Maggie Ellis, Chief Justice-elect, Supreme Court

Elected November 3, 2026, over the incumbent, Republican Chief Justice Jimmy Blacklock. The Associated Press called the race. The posted results are unofficial and not certified. The canvass, the official count, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

In the one education case we found from her time on the Third Court of Appeals, Ellis joined a 2025 decision on teachers' rights at partner-run campuses, and the Supreme Court is now reviewing it.

On that court, an intermediate appeals court in Austin, Ellis joined a panel opinion holding that district-employed teachers at partner-run campuses keep their statutory rights. The panel struck two parts of the commissioner's rule and upheld three. The Supreme Court heard argument on October 7, 2026, and has not ruled.

There doesn't appear to be a public record of her statements on education policy, teacher certification included, though we could not read her social-media accounts. The Houston Chronicle editorial board wrote that she and Blacklock "were circumspect about speaking directly to issues that may appear before them."

Background and powers of the office

Ellis was "elected to the Texas Third Court of Appeals in 2024," as her official biography puts it, and has served on that court since January 2025, the Tribune guide said.

Before that, she was an administrative law judge at the State Office of Administrative Hearings, a Travis County assistant district attorney and a lawyer in family, juvenile and child-welfare law. Her campaign site adds that she is immediate past chair of the State Bar's Juvenile Law Section.

She has described herself as a former teacher. She told Spectrum News on December 10, 2019: "I graduated from UT with a degree in education, then I worked as a teacher." Her court biography lists her as PTA president and vice president in the Leander Independent School District, or Leander ISD, and as a member of a Leander ISD zoning board, not as an employee there; her campaign biography describes those ties differently, as the statements below show.

A Supreme Court justice votes on which cases the court takes and on how it decides them, as the Tribune guide explained. The Code of Judicial Conduct limits the pledges that candidates for the court may make, as the section on the court above sets out.

Other: her teaching background. Her campaign presents her as a former teacher. Her campaign home page quotes her: "As a Justice on the Third Court of Appeals, a former teacher, foster mom, and PTA President, I have been a strong advocate for compassion and justice for our community."

Her campaign and court biographies describe her Leander ISD ties differently. The campaign biography says "she worked in public education through Leander ISD", while the court biography lists PTA and zoning-board roles there, not employment.

She told The Daily Texan on November 21, 2024: "It was really working with kids in the classroom that I knew something wasn't right at home."

Her court biography also lists "federal education law" among the subjects of her hearings, trials and appeals. It names no case or client.

Chari Kelly, Justice-elect, Supreme Court Place 2

Elected November 3, 2026, over the incumbent, Republican Justice James P. Sullivan, who was appointed in 2025. The Associated Press called the race. The posted results are unofficial and not certified. The canvass, the official count, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Kelly wrote the 2022 appeals-court opinion that affirmed an injunction for school districts against the governor's order barring local mask requirements, and the Supreme Court later vacated the judgment.

The case asked the Third Court of Appeals, an intermediate appeals court in Austin, whether that order validly suspended the Education Code powers districts relied on to require masks. Kelly wrote the court's opinion, which affirmed the injunction for the districts and held "the Governor does not possess absolute authority under the Texas Disaster Act to preempt orders issued by governmental entities and officials". The Supreme Court vacated the judgment on June 30, 2023.

Her campaign site republishes those words. Apart from them, there doesn't appear to be a public record of her statements on education policy, teacher certification included, though we could not read her social-media accounts. Her only rulings on educator certification were two procedural dismissals in 2020.

Kristen Hawkins, Justice-elect, Supreme Court Place 7

Elected November 3, 2026, over the incumbent, Republican Justice Kyle Hawkins, who was appointed in 2025. The Associated Press called the race. The posted results are unofficial and not certified. The canvass, the official count, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Three school-related cases came from Hawkins's Harris County trial court, and the Supreme Court docket names her as the judge in one of them.

Those three are the cases our appellate-docket searches found, and we read only the first page of each result list. Hawkins has been judge of the 11th District Court in Harris County since 2017. In one case, her court ruled on whether substantial evidence supported the commissioner of education's approval of a teacher's firing. It reversed the commissioner and sent the case back, and the Fourteenth Court of Appeals affirmed in 2023. We could not confirm her personal role in that ruling. Another case does name her: the Supreme Court lists her as the trial judge in a contractor's delay-damages suit over a county education department facility, where a petition is pending.

There doesn't appear to be a public record of her statements on education policy, teacher preparation and certification included.

Gisela D. Triana, Justice-elect, Supreme Court Place 8

Elected November 3, 2026, over the incumbent, Republican Justice Brett Busby. The Associated Press called the race. The posted results are unofficial and not certified. The canvass, the official count, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Triana wrote the 2020 appeals-court opinion that affirmed an injunction for Houston's school district against the commissioner's planned takeover, and the Supreme Court reversed it in 2023.

We found more school rulings by Triana than by any of the other three new justices. In the Houston case, she wrote the opinion on whether the district's claims against the commissioner overcame the state's immunity and whether a temporary injunction was proper. The opinion affirmed the injunction, and the Supreme Court reversed it on January 13, 2023, noting that the Legislature had since rewritten the governing law.

Five of her rulings concern educator licensing. Three of those are her reviews, as a trial judge, of certificate revocations by the State Board for Educator Certification, or SBEC, which licenses and disciplines educators. Outside her rulings, there doesn't appear to be a public record of her statements on education policy, teacher certification included; the statements of hers that we found concern the court in general.

Background and powers of the office

Triana has sat in Place 6 of the Third Court of Appeals, an intermediate appeals court in Austin, since her election in 2018. Before that, her official biography says, she "served for 14 years as the 200th District Court Judge" in Travis County, a post she took in 2005.

The Texas Tribune guide lists her earlier judgeships, from 1994 to 2004: justice of the peace, Austin municipal judge and county court-at-law judge. Earlier still, she was a prosecutor in the Travis County Attorney's Office, a staff attorney in the Secretary of State's elections division, and a criminal and family lawyer. She has also served on the Travis County Juvenile Board, the Travis County Child Protective Services Board and the Children's Justice Act Task Force. A Texas Tribune article from 2020 shows her as the Democratic nominee for the same seat that year.

As a trial judge she heard state education cases. Third Court opinions in appeals from Travis County involving the Texas Education Agency, or TEA, and SBEC name her as the presiding trial judge, and the Hudspeth appeal is one of them.

The Tribune guide describes the job: a Supreme Court justice votes on which cases the court takes and on how it decides them. The Code of Judicial Conduct bars judges and judicial candidates from pledges that would suggest how they would decide a class of cases.

There is a second account of the 2010 grading case. One research summary, whose cited Texas Tribune page no longer loads, describes an August 2010 denial of a temporary injunction to the districts. We could not tell whether that is the same ruling, and we found no order or cause number for it.

Teacher preparation and certification. Five of her rulings concern educator licensing. Three are her trial-court reviews of SBEC certificate revocations: she upheld the revocation in Gomez and reversed it in Lange and Tran, and the Third Court reversed both of those rulings. The other two are Third Court rulings: the A+ Texas Teachers order on the alternative-certification provider and her separate opinion in Caddo Mills.

In that concurrence, she wrote that "the school district's abrupt change in its course of dealing with an educator who had been employed by the district for 15 years in the same position, absent any cause, is the type of unfair surprise that borders on being unconscionable." She called the district's use of "an additional certification that had not previously been required" "disturbing". Both passages are words from a ruling on the case before the court, not statements of policy.

Education-oriented backers

The endorsement lists of Texas AFT COPE, the political committee of the teachers union Texas AFT, and of the Texas State Teachers Association include no judicial candidates. The Texas AFL-CIO, a labor federation that includes teacher-union affiliates, endorsed her on July 21, 2026. That is a labor endorsement, not an education one.

O'Hanlon, Demerath & Castillo, an Austin law firm, gave her $1,000 on November 27, 2023, in an earlier Third Court campaign. Among its practices, the firm's website lists "School District Social Media Litigation" and "Higher Education".

The Texas Home School Coalition endorsed her opponent, Busby.

State Board of Education

The State Board of Education and what it controls

The State Board of Education decides what Texas public-school students are taught and which teaching materials the state approves, and it can veto new charter schools and reject the rules for certifying teachers. Its 15 members are each "elected from districts", under Education Code §7.101, and the law sets out each of its powers:

  • Curriculum standards. The board sets what each subject must teach. Under §28.002(c), it "shall by rule identify the essential knowledge and skills of each subject of the required curriculum". Texas calls these standards the TEKS, and the same section ties instructional materials and state tests to them. The board also sets graduation requirements, under §7.102(c)(4).
  • Instructional materials. The Texas Education Agency, the state agency that runs public education, sends materials to the board for review, and the board keeps lists of approved and rejected materials under §§31.022, 31.024. Districts may not use materials it rejects.
  • Permanent School Fund. The board oversees the investment of the fund, the state's endowment for public schools. Section 43.003 says it "may invest the permanent school fund" under the Texas Constitution. Since a 2021 law, though, it has delegated day-to-day investment to the Texas Permanent School Fund Corporation, and five of that corporation's nine board members are State Board members, under §§43.052, 43.053.
  • Charter veto. The commissioner of education, who heads the Texas Education Agency, proposes new charter schools, and the board can veto them. A proposed charter takes effect unless, within 90 days, "a majority of the members of the board present and voting vote against the grant", under §12.101(b-0). The board may not vote on a charter the commissioner has not proposed.
  • Educator-certification rules. The rules for preparing and certifying teachers come from the State Board for Educator Certification, a separate state board, which must send every rule it proposes to the State Board of Education. The board can reject those rules but not change them. Under §21.042, it "may reject a proposed rule by a vote of at least two-thirds of the members of the board present and voting" within 90 days but "may not modify" it, and a rule it does not reject takes effect. Its review of the certification rules in June 2026 shows what they cover: the School Initiatives committee minutes of June 25, 2026 list admission to teacher-preparation programs, the programs themselves, certification exams and certificates.

An October 16, 2026, Texas Tribune voter guide wrote that the board passed "sweeping changes to social studies" for kindergarten through high school that year and "approved a new required reading list that includes Bible stories".

After the November 3, 2026, election, Democrats hold seven seats and Republicans seven, and the District 8 race is not called, in the Associated Press results on the Texas Tribune. The results stay unofficial on the Secretary of State's results page until the state canvass, the official count, ends on December 7, 2026.

For most board decisions, the record does not show how each member voted. The board's minutes record most decisions only as "carried" or as a tally such as 8-7, so a member's individual vote is on record for a minority of decisions. The vote tables below mark the rest "not recorded".
