Thomas Ray Garcia, State Board of Education, District 2

Won a seat held by Republicans. The Associated Press called the race for Garcia over Republican Victoria Hinojosa, as the Texas Tribune's results page shows. The result is not certified.

In brief

Garcia, a college English teacher who has never held elected office, campaigned against the state's voucher program and the state-written Bluebonnet Learning curriculum.

The seat is one of 15 on the State Board of Education, the elected board that sets curriculum standards. The board can reject, but not change, teacher-certification rules under Section 21.042.

His platform opposes both the voucher program and Bluebonnet Learning, the state-written reading and math materials. His survey answer on Bluebonnet was narrower: it criticized the materials but did not pledge to remove them.

On teacher certification, he wrote that the board should be able to amend the rules, which would take a change in the law.

Background and powers of the office

Garcia teaches English at South Texas College, where the Texas Tribune voter guide lists him as an adjunct professor and professor in 2022-23 and again since 2024. Before that, the same guide lists him as a teacher in the Pharr-San Juan-Alamo school district in 2016-17 and an instructor at UCLA in 2018-20. The guide also lists a college-access nonprofit he founded and directed from 2013 to 2023, the College Scholarship Leadership Access Program.

He has held no elected office. Teach the Vote, the candidate-information site of the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, shows him running unopposed in the March 2026 Democratic primary in its primary results. ATPE is a teacher association, and it "does not endorse candidates", its site says.

The State Board of Education, or SBOE, has 15 seats under Education Code §7.101. Its powers are set out at the start of this section.

Record by issue

General notes

Social media

We read eight posts on his Bluesky account, thomasraygarcia.bsky.social.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

Vouchers. His campaign platform page, which is undated and which we read on November 9, 2026, says: "I am against our state's school voucher program." The page adds, "I support school choice in the form of open-enrollment public schools," and gives the reason: "The solution to improving our public schools is to invest more, not to defund them through voucher programs".

Social media

  • Vouchers and funding. He posted on Bluesky on June 3, 2026: "At a time when public education is being underfunded and privatized, I couldn't stand aside".

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

His survey answer called for doubling the basic allotment, the state's base funding per student, and his platform supports higher pay for school workers. In ATPE's 2026 candidate survey on Teach the Vote, he wrote: "Our state's basic allotment should be doubled, affixed to inflation, and based on student enrollment rather than attendance." His platform says, "I support pay increases for school workers".

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

Testing and accountability. He opposes using the state test to rate schools and wants the elected board consulted on accountability changes. On STAAR, the state's standardized tests, his platform says: "I am against using the STAAR to grade public schools’ accountability scores". Of House Bill 8 of 2025, the testing law, he wrote on Teach the Vote: "I do not believe the Commissioner should have the authority to remove or change accountability indicators without consulting the elected SBOE".

Charter schools

Campaign pledge

He would keep the board's power over new charters. On Teach the Vote, he answered: "Yes, the SBOE should retain its authority to veto or approve new charter applications on a simple majority vote".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Curriculum, library books and religion. His platform opposes Bluebonnet Learning, the reading and math materials the Texas Education Agency wrote under House Bill 1605 of 2023. It says: "I am against the state-developed Bluebonnet Learning curriculum."

His answer on Teach the Vote was narrower: "I would ensure the Bluebonnet Learning instructional materials are error-free, pedagogically-sound, developmentally-appropriate, and student-centered ... Unfortunately, Bluebonnet Learning is currently none of these things." It did not pledge to remove the materials from the approved list. In the same answer, he opposed the extra state money for districts that adopt the materials, writing, "I believe in local control".

  • On the 2025-26 social studies rewrite, his Teach the Vote answer asked for "Much more weight than the SBOE is currently giving educators" and for content advisors with classroom experience.
  • On library books, his platform says: "I believe local communities should have the freedom to decide what books belong in their own school libraries".

Social media

  • Curriculum. The next day, June 4, 2026, he wrote: "When we flip this seat in November, I will listen to educators, not extremists, on how to prepare our students for the future".

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

He wants the board to have more power over certification rules than the law now gives it. Those rules come from the State Board for Educator Certification, or SBEC, the separate board that proposes them. Asked about the board's power over the rules, he wrote on Teach the Vote: "Yes. The SBOE is a duly-elected body, and it serves as an important check on the rulemaking actions. The SBOE should also have the ability to amend specific provisions of rules back to the SBEC rather than simply approve or veto rules". Section 21.042 bars the State Board of Education from changing those rules, so his proposal would take a change in the law.

His platform also takes up the Reading Academies, the reading training for teachers that came out of House Bill 3, the 2019 school finance law: "That's why I’ll fight to reform the Reading Academies so they actually help educators improve reading outcomes." The platform says he would phase out "online-only modules in favor of skilled trainers" and seek "funding for math and literacy coaches, math and literacy training for teachers".

Higher education

Campaign pledge

His platform says: "College for all? No. College access for all? Yes."

Coretta Mallet-Fontenot, State Board of Education, District 4

Won the unexpired term that runs to 2028. The Associated Press called the race over Republican Tammie Nielsen, whom Gov. Greg Abbott appointed to the seat in August, as the Texas Tribune's results page and voter guide show. The result is not certified.

In brief

Mallet-Fontenot urged a House committee in 2025 to vote down a voucher bill, wrote in 2022 that she would limit new charter applications, and in 2019 co-signed an op-ed against a state takeover of Houston schools.

Her campaign calls her a "27 year Houston ISD educator", and she now works for the Houston teachers' union. The seat she won is on the elected State Board of Education, which sets curriculum standards.

Her comment on the voucher bill was written for a House committee hearing in March 2025. In 2022 she wrote that she would limit new charter applications, and in 2026 she said the board can "increase charter school financial and academic accountability". The 2019 op-ed connected the takeover to charters: it said a state takeover would lead to "irreversible and discriminatory chartering of schools in black and brown communities".

She has never held an office with recorded votes on education policy. But in 2021, as a member of a Houston district advisory committee, she voted against a plan with exemptions for hiring noncertified vocational teachers.

Background and powers of the office

Her campaign site describes her as a "27 year Houston ISD educator", meaning the Houston Independent School District, and lists elementary, middle-school and high-school teaching, literacy coaching and testing coordination. She now works for the Houston Federation of Teachers, the Houston teachers' union, as "Organizer / Teacher Leader Program Director".

She has run for this seat before. In the 2022 District 4 Democratic runoff she lost to Staci Childs, 41.9% to 58.1%. Four years later, a post by Texas AFT, the state affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers, said the district's precinct chairs, who are local party officials, had chosen her for the 2026 ballot on August 15, 2026.

The seat carries the State Board of Education's powers, set out at the start of this section, under Education Code §7.101.

Record by issue

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Statement or interview

  • Vouchers. For the House Public Education Committee's hearing of March 11, 2025, on House Bill 3, a voucher bill, she sent written comment, printed on page 923 of the public comments: "This bill would take funds out of the schools that service my family members. Please vote no on HB3". The voucher program that became law came from a different bill, the Senate's SB 2.

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

Her 2022 answer and her current site ask for the same two things: pay raises and fully funded pre-kindergarten. Her campaign site says she believes in "fully-funded PreK, pay raises for school employees". Four years earlier, answering the League of Women Voters on page 19 of the 2022 runoff guide, she listed "1) fully funded public education 2) pay raises for school employees 3) fully funded pre-kindergarten".

Statement or interview

  • Teacher pay. Two years earlier she had sent written comment on Senate Bill 9 of 2023. Her comment of May 9, 2023, on page 75 of the public comments, said: "We deserve and have earned a raise; not a one-time bonus" and "Many of my colleagues are frustrated and contemplating leaving the profession due to the low pay".

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

Testing and state takeovers. Her campaign criticizes the state test and decisions made by noneducators. Its site says: "Dr. Coretta understands that standardized tests, like the STAAR, do not accurately measure intelligence," and "we cannot allow noneducators to make important decisions that govern the direction of our school communities".

The pledge on the Houston takeover is in Texas AFT's words, not hers. The union wrote on August 21, 2026 that she "plans to hold TEA Commissioner Mike Morath accountable for his takeover of Houston ISD". In that takeover, announced in 2019, the state put the Houston district under "an agency-run board of managers" in place of the elected board, in the words of Teach the Vote, the candidate-information site of the Association of Texas Professional Educators.

Statement or interview

  • State takeover, charters and testing. On May 3, 2019, she co-signed a Houston Chronicle op-ed that said: "A state takeover would lead to irreversible and discriminatory chartering of schools in black and brown communities". It added: "The charter model is simply incompatible with a public school system committed to serving all students". Seven years later the Chronicle's editorial board interviewed her, and its piece of October 10, 2026 quoted her: "Teachers now are having to fight or mitigate the ills of poverty". The board wrote that she "had few kind words for HISD Superintendent Mike Miles".

Charter schools

Campaign pledge

Her answers have called for limits on new charters and said the board can increase charter accountability. In 2022 she wrote, on page 19 of the guide: "I would limit new charter applications. Charter schools received an additional $1,058 per student". In 2026 she said in the League of Women Voters Houston guide that the board can "increase charter school financial and academic accountability".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Curriculum. Both guides have her asking for curriculum built on facts, and both name history. On the TEKS, the state's curriculum standards, she wrote in 2022, on page 19: "The TEKS should be objectively written and research-based by history teachers, so students learn the facts of our history". In 2026 she called for "fact based curriculum materials across grade/content areas, particularly in history and science" in the League of Women Voters Houston guide.

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

In the same 2026 guide, she said the board can "fund educator mentor programs to retain educators".

Statement or interview

  • Teacher training. An ABC13 report of September 16, 2020, on Houston's virtual learning, quoted her: "I definitely think more training for the HUB is definitely needed".

Voting record

She has never held an office with recorded votes on education policy, but she has voted on a Houston district plan. In March 2021, as an employee member of the district's District Advisory Committee, an advisory body, she voted against a District of Innovation plan, the kind of plan that lets a school district exempt itself from some state rules. A Houston Chronicle article of April 2, 2021 said this plan included exemptions for "the hiring of noncertified vocational teachers". The committee rejected it 21-10, and the same article quoted her: "I don’t think the district’s intention necessarily matters when you look at the law".

Education-oriented backers

Teacher organizations. Texas AFT's political committee listed her for the November 2026 general election as of October 1, in an archived copy of its list. The Texas State Teachers Association did not: she is not on its lists, including its general-election list. Her campaign site adds four union presidents as individual endorsers: Jackie Anderson of the Houston Federation of Teachers, Candis Houston of Aldine AFT, Zeph Capo of Texas AFT and Shonda Below of Northeast AFT.

Money. The Houston Federation of Teachers, the union she works for, gave $1,000 on October 16, 2026, for the general election, and the gift appears in her report as well.

Advocacy groups. Community Voices for Public Education, a Houston public-school group, endorsed her and said it "will be supporting our endorsed candidates through block-walks, phone banking, donations". That is a stated plan, not a record of work done. The Texas Freedom Network endorsed every Democrat on the board ballot.

Charter or choice groups. Charter Schools Now PAC gave her opponent, Nielsen, $1,000 on September 14, 2026.

Allison Bush, State Board of Education, District 5

Won an open seat held by Democrat Rebecca Bell-Metereau, who retired. The Associated Press called the race over Republican Mica Arellano, as the Texas Tribune's results page shows. The result is not certified.

In brief

Bush opposes the unlimited expansion of charter schools but counts them as part of public education, and she wrote that the board should keep its power to veto certification rules.

She won an open seat on the elected State Board of Education, which sets curriculum standards. Her campaign site opposes unlimited charter growth, and in a survey answer she wrote that charter schools are part of the state's public education system.

Her answer on vouchers says public funds must strengthen classrooms, but it does not call for repealing the voucher program.

On certification, she wrote that the board should keep its power to review and veto the certification board's rules.

Background and powers of the office

The Texas Tribune voter guide listed Bush as a bond-election coordinator at Gallagher Construction since 2021 and, from 2011 to 2019, executive director of foundation and development for the Pflugerville school district.

Her campaign's FAQ page says that in the early 2000s she taught in Austin with American YouthWorks, which the Austin Chronicle called "the charter school American YouthWorks".

Her page on Teach the Vote, the candidate-information site of the Association of Texas Professional Educators, shows that she advanced to a May 26, 2026, runoff in the Democratic primary.

Her seat on the State Board of Education, or SBOE, carries the powers set out at the start of this section, under Education Code §7.101.

Record by issue

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

Vouchers. Her undated FAQ page posts her answer to a Democratic club's questionnaire, in which she wrote that public funds, "including vouchers", "must strengthen classrooms, not corporate profits". The answer does not call for repealing the state's voucher program.

Campaign pledge

Curriculum, library books and religion. Her answers favor optional state materials, criticize book bans and limit religion in the curriculum to teaching about it.

Education-oriented backers

Teacher organizations. Texas AFT and the Texas State Teachers Association both endorsed her for the general election, and Education Austin endorsed her as well. Money. Teacher groups gave to her runoff and general-election campaigns, and on each item the payer's report and hers differ in amount, date or form.

  • The Texas State Teachers Association PAC gave on April 9, 2026, which by date falls in the runoff. The amount is $2,000 in the PAC's report and $2,500 in hers, on the same day.
  • For the May 2026 runoff, the Association of Texas Professional Educators PAC gave $2,500, dated May 12 in its report and May 16 in hers. This was a contribution, not an endorsement.
  • The Texas State Teachers Association PAC gave again for the general election: $1,000, dated August 13 in its report and August 20 in hers.
  • Texas AFT COPE's $1,200 for the general election appears in two forms. The payer's report lists "Public event sponsorship" on September 12, an in-kind item, meaning goods or services rather than money, and her report lists a $1,200 contribution on September 14.

Advocacy groups. The Texas Freedom Network endorsed every Democrat on the board ballot in its slate.

Charter or choice groups. Charter Schools Now PAC endorsed and funded her runoff opponent, Stephanie Limon Bazan.

Michelle Palmer, State Board of Education, District 6

Won a seat held by Republicans. The Associated Press called the race over Republican Tiffany Nelson, and Palmer led by about 1.4 percentage points in unofficial returns, as the Texas Tribune's results page shows. The result is not certified.

In brief

Palmer, a history and government teacher who lost this race in 2020 and 2022, vowed in 2022 to vote against all new charter applications and in 2026 called for pausing approvals.

This time she won a Republican-held seat on the elected State Board of Education, which sets curriculum standards. In 2026 she wrote that she would pause new charter approvals until current charters are audited. On vouchers, in a 2020 questionnaire, she answered "Strongly Disagree" to a statement supporting school choice, including vouchers.

She has also linked certification to her opposition to charters, and on certification rules she wrote that she favors the elected board over the appointed certification board.

Background and powers of the office

The Texas Tribune voter guide listed Palmer as a history and government teacher who has taught since 2009.

Her page on Teach the Vote, a site run by the Association of Texas Professional Educators, a teacher association, shows that she was the Democratic nominee for this seat in 2020 and 2022 and lost both times.

A post by Texas AFT, the state affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers, names her as a member of Aldine AFT, a local teachers' union. She has held no public office.

The seat carries the powers of the State Board of Education, or SBOE, that are set out at the start of this section, under Education Code §7.101.

Record by issue

General notes

Social media

We checked her Bluesky account, rabidreader1970.bsky.social, which had 978 feed items, seven of them her own posts. On November 11, 2025, she posted there: "I signed this petition organized by Texas Freedom Network". The petition was about the board's social studies overhaul.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

Vouchers. In 2020 she answered a questionnaire from iVoterGuide, a voter guide run by AFA Action that says it informs faith-based voters. To the statement "I support school choice, including voucher programs, tax credits, charter schools, private schools, and home schools", she answered "Strongly Disagree".

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

Testing. She has written against required testing and against moving power from the elected board to the state agency. In 2022 she wrote on Teach the Vote: "I suggest we get rid of testing (at least not require it for graduation) and instead use a portfolio system." In 2026 she wrote there about the Texas Education Agency, or TEA, the state agency that runs public education: "Elected board members have been slowly having their power stripped and given to the appointed TEA. I am against this completely".

Charter schools

Campaign pledge

She wrote against new charters in both her 2022 and 2026 surveys on Teach the Vote. The 2022 answer was a vow: "I have vowed to vote against all new charter school applications." The 2026 answer proposed a pause: "I would put a pause on new charter approvals until the current charter systems can be audited".

Statement or interview

  • Charters and reading lists. The Houston Chronicle editorial board's piece of October 10, 2026, quoted her: "Should kids in Amarillo be reading the same thing my students in Aldine are reading? ... I don't think they should." The editorial board wrote that she was open to charters "dedicated to certain populations, such as kids with special education needs" and would otherwise seek "a moratorium on new charter school systems".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Curriculum. Her 2026 survey on Teach the Vote asks for climate change in the science standards: "Science standards need to include climate change for instance". Her undated platform page, which still describes the 2022 race, says "Moses should not be mentioned in the US History curriculum" and supports "actively teaching consent".

On state-written materials she pointed to her own courses, which use open educational resources (OER), teaching materials that are openly licensed. She wrote on Teach the Vote: "I use OER materials as my textbook in all of my courses and none of them are TEA developed".

Statement or interview

  • Sex education. Six years earlier, in October 2020, she said in OutSmart: "Abstinence-only sex education is failing the students of Texas".

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

She favors the elected board over the appointed certification board and has linked certification to her charter position. The rules come from the State Board for Educator Certification, or SBEC, which proposes them. In 2026 she wrote of those rules on Teach the Vote: "SBOE is elected whereas SBEC is appointed. I will always choose the more accountable and pro-democracy way to do things".

She made the link to charters in her 2022 survey on Teach the Vote. One reason she gave there for opposing charters was that they "do not require teacher certification and do not give yearly contracts". In the same survey she wrote that educators and groups such as the association "should be met with regarding who to appoint to curriculum committees, revising of teacher certification requirements, and revising of graduation requirements".

In 2026 she said the board "should help to improve certification pathways to increase the number of trained and certified teachers in TX", in the League of Women Voters Houston guide.

Statement or interview

  • Teachers. In a Texas Tribune story of October 22, 2026, she said: "Teachers see what's happening, and they're kind of sick of it".

Voting record

Palmer has never held an office with recorded votes.

Education-oriented backers

Teacher organizations. Texas AFT endorsed her on July 24, 2026, and the Texas State Teachers Association endorsed her for the general election on its endorsement list.

Labor endorsement. The Texas AFL-CIO, the state labor federation, endorsed her in the same announcement. That is a labor endorsement, not an education one.

Money, November 2026 general election. Texas AFT COPE and the Texas State Teachers Association PAC gave to her general-election campaign, and the two sides' reports date each gift differently.

  • Texas AFT COPE gave $5,000, dated October 5 in the payer's report and October 2 in hers.
  • The Texas State Teachers Association PAC's $250 is dated August 13 in the PAC's report and October 2 in hers.
  • In an earlier cycle, iVoterGuide lists money she received in 2020 from the Association of Texas Professional Educators.

Advocacy groups. Community Voices for Public Education, a Houston public-school group, endorsed her, and so did the Texas Freedom Network, in its slate.

Charter or choice groups. Her opponent, Nelson, received a $2,500 contribution and $32,483 in in-kind digital ads, help given as goods or services rather than money, from Charter Schools Now PAC, as one report and another show. Nelson also received in-kind texting from Texans for Educational Freedom, and the Tribune guide gave a figure of $90,387, including the texting.

Tiffany Clark, State Board of Education, District 13 (re-elected)

Re-elected. The Associated Press called the race over Republican Carlos "Charlie" Garza, as the Texas Tribune's results page shows. The result is not certified. After the March primary, a post by the Association of Texas Professional Educators on its Teach the Vote site named a different Republican opponent, April Moore. We did not resolve the difference.

In brief

On the votes the minutes record by name, Clark opposed the new social studies standards, the 2026 reading list and every charter applicant but one.

Clark sits on the elected State Board of Education, which sets curriculum standards. The January 2025 minutes also place her on its Committee on School Initiatives, which reviews the charter applications and every rule the certification board proposes.

She voted no on the 2026 required reading list, which includes Bible passages, and on every recorded vote on the social studies standards. In 2025 and 2026 she also voted against allowing every charter applicant that came to a named roll call, with one exception, Unidos Soccer Leadership Academy.

All three of her recorded votes on certification rules were against rejecting a rule. Two of them were her own committee motions, which let rule packages take effect in January and September 2025. The minutes do not record by name how she voted on the packages that followed, including the 2026 rules written to carry out House Bill 2 of 2025.

Background and powers of the office

Clark was a middle- and high-school counselor for 10 years and served on the board of the DeSoto Independent School District from 2017 to May 2023, as its vice president in 2021-2022.

Her board biography shows that she took her seat on the State Board of Education on January 1, 2025, for an unexpired term, and says she is an adjunct professor at the University of North Texas at Dallas, "where she teaches future educators".

On the board she sits on the Committee on School Initiatives. That committee reviews the charter applications and every rule proposed by the State Board for Educator Certification, the separate board that writes certification rules. The board's powers, under Education Code §7.101, are described at the start of this section.

Record by issue

General notes

Campaign pledge

Her undated campaign home page pledges to "Advocate for a balanced curriculum that includes an improved testing instrument aligned with Texas standards," to "Fight for the mental health of students, staff, and teachers," and "STOP BOOK BANS!"

She did not answer the association's 2026 survey on Teach the Vote, and the 2024 League of Women Voters guide lists her as unopposed, with no answers.

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Statement or interview

Testing and teacher preparation. In 2024 she questioned tests as a measure of students and teachers. For the House Public Education Committee's August 13, 2024 hearing on teacher certification, she submitted written comment saying that teachers take on debt for more education without more pay, and that "it takes more than a test to define a student or teacher. When we talk about teacher certification it has to go back to standards at the home..." She also wrote that STAAR, the state's standardized test, "isn't relatable to all students".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Statement or interview

Curriculum and religion. She has criticized the social studies draft and the Bible passages on the reading list.

  • In board debate on the draft social studies standards, known as the TEKS, on April 10, 2026, she said: "It seems as if, when it comes to Black and brown information being in these TEKS, we continue to undermine our experiences".
  • In a June 2026 CNN report on the reading list with Bible passages, she said that she and some Christian constituents believe "Bible lessons should be taught on Sundays". She also said: "Teachers know what their students need... Our students need to focus on reading comprehension".
  • In November 2024, before she was seated, the Texas Freedom Network reported that "Clark said she would've voted against the curriculum," meaning Bluebonnet Learning, the reading and math materials written by the Texas Education Agency.

Voting record

In 2025 and 2026 she voted against allowing every charter applicant that came to a named roll call except one. She voted against seven named applicants. She voted against allowing six of them, Mater Academy San Antonio, Arcadia High School, Fort Worth STEAM Academy, Frank Liu Jr. Academy, Museum School of East Dallas and Texas High School for Accelerated Learning, and the board allowed all six. She voted to veto the seventh, Valenta Academy, and the board vetoed it 10-3-1. The exception was Unidos Soccer Leadership Academy, which she voted to allow in committee on June 25, 2025, a motion defeated 5-9. Two days later, on June 27, 2025, she voted not to veto it, and the board vetoed it 9-4-1. She was absent for the committee vote on the 2026 charter list.

She voted no on all seven recorded votes on the social studies standards, from the course sequence in September 2025 to the grade 8 standards in June 2026, and all seven passed. For two of them, her vote is as reported by the Tribune. She also voted no on the 2026 reading list, which the board adopted 9-5-1, and on the January 2025 motions to strike or reject parts of the engineering career-course standards. She voted against removing all Houghton Mifflin Harcourt products from the approved materials list, a motion defeated 3-11.

Her votes on the American Indian/Native Studies course were yes in committee, no on postponing it and yes on suspending the rules to take it up. The minutes do not record her vote on final approval, which carried 9-5.

As the committee member who made the motions, she let two packages of certification rules take effect. In April 2025 she also voted against the committee's veto of a rule on special-education assignments. That veto carried 3-2 in committee but was defeated 4-9 at the board, and the rule took effect. Certification-rule decisions before 2025 predate her service. Where the minutes do not show her individual vote, the table says "not recorded".

On training for school trustees, she voted no on the parental-rights rule at first reading in January 2026 and yes on the substitute package in April 2026. In committee in April 2025 she cast three no votes on the "Framework for Governance Leadership", and each motion carried 3-2.

33 rows

As a DeSoto school board member. A Dallas Morning News story shows that on August 30, 2020, as the district faced possible state oversight, she voted against accepting the superintendent's resignation agreement and against naming an acting superintendent. Both motions carried 4-3. The district credits her with adding "African-American and Mexican American studies courses to the district curriculum".

Education-oriented backers

Teacher organizations. Texas AFT, the state affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers, endorsed her through its political committee for both the March 2026 primary round and the general election. She appears on its May 26 list and its October 1 list, in archived copies. The Texas State Teachers Association endorsed her for the general election on its endorsement list.

Money. Her own report lists one teacher-group contribution, and the Texas State Teachers Association PAC reports two more that do not appear in her reports.

  • The Texas American Federation of Teachers gave her $250 on September 18, 2024, for the November 2024 general election, as her report shows.
  • The Texas State Teachers Association PAC reports giving her $1,000 on February 19, 2026, for the March primary, and $500 on August 13, 2026, for the general election. Neither appears in her own reports through October 24, 2026, and we did not establish why.

Advocacy groups. The Texas Freedom Network endorsed every Democrat on the board ballot in its announcement. Her own campaign endorsements page is empty.

Dana Van de Walker, candidate, State Board of Education, District 8

Race not called. She led the Republican incumbent, Audrey G. Young, by 569 votes in Associated Press data on November 9, 2026. The incumbent has not conceded, as the Texas Tribune shows. The Houston Chronicle reported on November 5, 2026, that the margin was within the range for a recount if Young requested one.

In brief

Van de Walker, whose race is not called, wrote that alternative certification should be the exception and that charter schools also need certified teachers.

She ran for the District 8 seat on the elected State Board of Education, which sets curriculum standards, and has never held an office with recorded votes. Her views on certification come from her survey answers on Teach the Vote and in a League of Women Voters guide.

In those answers she also wrote that she would fight to remove the Ten Commandments and religiously influenced curriculum from public schools, and she backed an across-the-board raise for teachers and an end to state school takeovers.

Background and powers of the office

Lone Star College's directory lists Van de Walker as its "Honors and International Director". The Houston Chronicle has said she teaches government there, and on February 15, 2026 it called her "a first-time candidate".

Her campaign site says she taught English as a second language in Korea and "earned her CELTA teaching certificate", and that she holds an Ed.D. in higher education leadership from 2021.

Her page on Teach the Vote, the candidate-information site of the Association of Texas Professional Educators, shows that she graded STAAR exams, the state's standardized tests, for ETS, a testing organization, from 2015 to 2018. None of these sources mentions a Texas K-12 classroom job or a Texas teaching certificate.

The District 8 seat carries the powers of the State Board of Education, or SBOE, described at the start of this section, under Education Code §7.101.

Record by issue

General notes

Social media

We could not read her Facebook campaign page or her Instagram and TikTok accounts, all named dana4txsboe8.

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

School funding and teacher pay; state takeovers. In the League of Women Voters Houston guide, she wrote: "I support an across-the-board increase in teacher salaries and an end to state school takeovers".

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

Testing. She wrote on Teach the Vote: "This experience taught me that we need greater oversight in our standardized testing AND that we need to develop more holistic approaches to student evaulation".

Charter schools

Campaign pledge

In her survey answer on Teach the Vote, she wrote that she would keep the board's veto and limit charter expansion "as they have historically been held to lower accountability standards". In the same answer she kept a place for charters as "an option for providing a highly-specialized curriculum, such as foreign language immersion".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Curriculum, library books and religion. She wrote on Teach the Vote: "I believe that religion has no place in our public schools and will fight to remove the Ten Commandments and any religiously-influenced curriculum ... I am also fiercely opposed to book bans".

In her survey answers on Teach the Vote and in the League of Women Voters Houston guide, she wrote that she favors state approval of common materials "by subject-matter experts" and would have "only 1-2 books" state-mandated per grade.

Statement or interview

  • Curriculum. A November 5, 2026, Houston Chronicle story summarized members' plans to amend the 2026 social studies standards, revisit the reading list and reevaluate Bluebonnet Learning, the state-written reading and math materials. It then quoted her: "We’ve been running with that as a day one promise ... We’re really committed to keeping the church out of our state and also uphold academic integrity". Earlier, in February 2026, the Chronicle's editorial board had written in an editorial that she is "far more worried about the subpar quality of the Bluebonnet curriculum". Her opponent, Young, answered her criticism of the standards in the Chronicle on October 10, 2026: "It’s always great to handpick one or two standards that you don’t like and inflame the information".

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

She wrote on Teach the Vote that alternative certification should be the exception and that every school the board oversees, charters included, needs certified teachers: "It is squarely the responsibility of the SBOE to ensure that our teachers are prepared to be in the classrooms ... Alternative certification programs, while useful, should be the exception, not the rule, in teacher certification. Similarly, I believe that all schools under the purview of the SBOE, including charter schools, need to have certified teachers in the classroom".

In the 2026 general-election League of Women Voters Houston guide, she wrote: "Texas has a teacher crisis. We have too few teachers overall, along with an unacceptable percentage of teachers coming into our districts without certification (or with alternate certification still in progress)".

Statement or interview

  • Teachers. A Polk County Enterprise story quoted her in Livingston on July 9, 2026: "A huge priority of mine is to recruit teachers, pay teachers and keep them here in Texas".

Higher education

Campaign pledge

Her home page lists "AFFORDABLE HIGHER EDUCATION FOR ALL" alongside "SEPARATION OF CHURCH AND STATE" and "INVESTMENT IN TEXAS PUBLIC SCHOOLS".

Voting record

Van de Walker has never held an office with recorded votes.

Education-oriented backers

Teacher organizations endorsed her, and a charter-school political committee gave to her opponent. Texas AFT, the state affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers, endorsed her on July 24, 2026. In the same announcement the Texas AFL-CIO, the state labor federation, also endorsed her; that is a labor endorsement, not an education one.

The Texas State Teachers Association put her on its endorsement list, and its PAC gave her $250 on August 13, 2026, for the general election. The gift appears in both the PAC's report and her own.

The Texas Freedom Network endorsed the full board slate. Her own endorsements page lists no education organization.

Young received $5,000 from Charter Schools Now PAC on April 28, 2025, plus later contributions and in-kind help, which is help given as goods or services rather than money. Young also received in-kind texting from Texans for Educational Freedom.

Marisa B. Pérez-Díaz, State Board of Education, District 3

Not on the 2026 ballot. Her term runs to January 1, 2029, her board biography says.

In brief

Pérez-Díaz wrote in 2018 that she wanted charter expansion halted pending an assessment, and from 2019 to 2025 she voted to allow some new charters and to veto others.

She has sat on the State Board of Education since 2013, and her board biography calls her "the most senior Democrat on the board".

In a 2018 survey she wrote that she wanted "a halt to the expansion of additional charter schools, until a proper assessment can be made". From 2019 to 2025 she voted to allow some charter applicants and to veto others.

On vouchers, in 2022 she voted for a board legislative priority that opposed diverting public dollars from public schools to vouchers.

She wrote in the same survey that the board's "authority to review and veto rule actions should remain intact" for educator-certification rules, and in 2014 she voted to reject a rule on candidates for teacher-preparation programs.

Background and powers of the office

Pérez-Díaz was elected in November 2012, took office in 2013 and was re-elected in 2014, 2018, 2022 and 2024. Her board biography says she worked at the Texas Department of Family and Protective Services, spent "nearly a decade as a district-level administrator in several Texas school districts," is now a vice president at Firstmark Credit Union and served as Marisa B. Perez until early 2017.

From 2017 to 2020 she was vice chair of the Committee on School Initiatives, which reviews certification rules. Since 2021 she has served on the School Finance/Permanent School Fund committee (the Permanent School Fund is the state endowment that helps pay for public schools), and the same biography says she was a founding director of the Texas Permanent School Fund Corporation. Committee minutes list her as vice chair of the School Finance/Permanent School Fund committee in 2025.

The board's powers, under §7.101 of the Education Code, are described at the start of this section.

Record by issue

General notes

Social media

The only site ATPE's profile lists for her is marisabperez.com, which is now a parked page.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

Vouchers. Her 2015 campaign page, written in the third person and now available as an archived copy, says that as a new member she "passionately debated and supported the State Board of Education's Anti-Voucher Resolution". We did not check the resolution's date.

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Statement or interview

Testing and state takeovers. In November 2019, after the state takeover of the Houston Independent School District was announced, she "questioned Morath regarding the process for transitioning from an agency-run board of managers back to a locally elected body," according to ATPE's account. Mike Morath is the commissioner of education.

Charter schools

Campaign pledge

The Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, a teacher association, posts candidates' survey answers on its candidate-information site, Teach the Vote. On charters, her 2018 answer reads: "Overall, the performance of charter schools is unimpressive... It would be my desire to see a halt to the expansion of additional charter schools, until a proper assessment can be made..."

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Curriculum. In the same survey she called the standards "mile wide and inch deep" and wrote that educators "must have a seat at the table".

Statement or interview

Curriculum and religion. Her statements below on curriculum concern three matters: the 2022 social studies delay, the Bluebonnet Learning materials and the 2026 high school standards.

  • After the board delayed the social studies rewrite in 2022, she wrote in a signed op-ed in the San Antonio Express-News on September 15, 2022: "On Sept. 2, the State Board of Education, or SBOE, failed our educators and students" and "We, the SBOE, are the gatekeepers. We should never be the groundskeepers".
  • FOX 7 Austin, covering the board's November 2024 debate on Bluebonnet Learning, a set of state-written instructional materials, quoted her: "Had it not been for the Christian bias in this content, I do really find value in how a lot of these lessons are laid out." ATPE reported that she also raised a "conflict of interest" in the agency being both a vendor and a reviewer of materials.
  • On the high school social studies standards, the Texas Tribune quoted her in August 2026: "Slavery is foundational to this country."

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

The same survey asked whether the State Board of Education, or SBOE, should keep its power over educator-certification rules, which the State Board for Educator Certification, or SBEC, writes. She answered: "Absolutely! SBEC is an appointed board and therefore is answerable to the Commissioner of Education. As an elected body, the SBOE has a responsibility and is accountable to our constituents... the authority to review and veto rule actions should remain intact".

She did not answer ATPE's 2022 or 2024 surveys.

Statement or interview

On certification, she has spoken about the 2022 edTPA decision and about uncertified teachers.

  • The board rejected edTPA, a performance assessment the certification board had adopted in place of the existing certification exam, and she then represented the board at a July 21, 2022 work session with the certification board. ATPE reported that she "noted that Option C was most aligned with the direction the SBOE wanted to take." That account described Option C as a performance assessment run as a preparation-program requirement rather than a certification exam.
  • In January 2025, ATPE wrote: "Responding to a question from Perez-Diaz, Morath clarified there is no requirement that newly hired uncertified teachers ever get certified."

Voting record

Charter votes and her 2018 statement, side by side. In 2018 she wrote on Teach the Vote that she wanted "a halt to the expansion of additional charter schools, until a proper assessment can be made". She voted to allow Gathering Place in 2019, Essence Prep, Rocketship and Thrive Center in 2021, and Celebrate Dyslexia and Up Excellence in 2023.

In 2025 she voted to allow Mater Academy San Antonio, Fort Worth STEAM Academy and Frank Liu Jr. Academy, and she voted in committee to allow Unidos Soccer Leadership Academy. She also voted to veto others, as the table shows. In June 2026 she voted against both charter decisions that came to a named vote: the 2026 Generation 31 list in committee and Texas High School for Accelerated Learning at the board.

One charter vote may be recorded differently elsewhere. For Royal Public Schools in 2020, the minutes list her among the no votes on allowing the charter, while a table by the Texas Association of School Administrators, a school administrators' group, reportedly lists her position as "Allow". We did not read that table.

On the social studies standards, she voted no on all seven recorded votes from September 2025 to June 2026, and all seven passed; for two of them her vote comes from Texas Tribune coverage. In September 2022 her own amendment to start from her alternative grades 6-8 framework failed 7-7, and she voted against both the framework the board approved and the delay. On Bluebonnet Learning in November 2024, her motion to remove the reading and language arts materials from consideration failed 7-8, and three days later she voted against keeping them on the approved list.

Three other named votes of hers differ from those of other Democrats on the board. She voted to keep Bluebonnet Math on the approved list, which passed 13-2 with Democrat Ortega voting no, as the minutes show. In 2023 she voted to change the abortion language in the materials review rubric from "describe" to "promote or encourage," while Democrats Bell-Metereau, Childs and Ortega abstained. And in 2014 she voted to reject a certification rule that Democrats Cortez and Dominguez voted to keep.

Of her votes on certification rules that the minutes record by name, that 2014 vote is the only one to reject a rule. Two other rejections, in 2018 and of edTPA in 2022, carried unanimously with no names recorded. In 2022 she voted to let the contract-abandonment rules take effect, and in 2023 she voted against vetoing the revised school librarian and reading specialist certificate rules, which the board rejected 10 to 5. As vice chair of the School Initiatives committee from 2017 to 2020, she moved to take no action on rules in ten chapters, and every one of those motions carried.

Education-oriented backers

The Texas State Teachers Association endorsed her for the November 2024 general election on its 2024 list, and its PAC sent her $500 on November 18, 2024. The check was never cashed and was voided on April 16, 2025.

Families for Education and Opportunity, a San Antonio political committee whose main purpose we could not establish, gave her $1,000 on October 20, 2025, off-cycle. The committee's own report shows its other 2025 gifts going mostly to San Antonio city candidates and to Republican board member Audrey Young.

ATPE's profile says that in 2018 she was "recommended favorably by Texans for Public Education," a group of educators, and endorsed in the primary by the San Antonio Express-News.

Gustavo Reveles, State Board of Education, District 1

Not on the 2026 ballot. His term runs to January 1, 2029, his board biography says.

In brief

Reveles urged a moratorium on charter expansion in 2024, and on the board he has voted against allowing every charter applicant that came to a named roll call in 2025 and 2026 except one.

He won his seat on the State Board of Education in November 2024 with 50.92% of the vote.

In a 2024 questionnaire he wrote, "I strongly oppose the use of vouchers, which would further diminish funding for public schools," and called for a moratorium on charter expansion. On the board, the only charter applicant he has voted to allow on a named roll call is Unidos Soccer Leadership Academy. He has also voted no each time the social studies standards came to a recorded vote; for two of those votes, his position comes from Texas Tribune coverage.

On certification, he wrote in a 2024 League of Women Voters guide that "Districts should have the option to rely on non-certified educators for hard-to-fill subjects," with proper certification to follow. His individual votes on certification rules are not recorded.

Background and powers of the office

Canutillo ISD and his board biography say Reveles spent 15 years as a journalist at the El Paso Times and the Fort Worth Star-Telegram and then moved to school-district communications, working for the Canutillo school district in 2010-2014 and the El Paso school district in 2014-2022. He went back to Canutillo in June 2022 and is now its executive director of communications.

The San Antonio Report, a San Antonio news site, shows him winning the seat in November 2024 with 50.92% of the vote. He took office on January 1, 2025, and the January 2025 minutes list him on the Committee on Instruction, which handles the curriculum standards.

The board's powers, under §7.101 of the Education Code, are described at the start of this section.

Record by issue

General notes

Social media

The only campaign site listed for him in 2024 was a Facebook group link, which we did not retrieve.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

Vouchers. In his 2024 San Antonio Report questionnaire, he wrote: "I strongly oppose the use of vouchers, which would further diminish funding for public schools."

Charter schools

Campaign pledge

In the same questionnaire, he wrote that the state should "place a moratorium on the expansion of charter programs until the public receives a true assessment of how charter schools are performing".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Curriculum and religion. In his 2024 answer in the League of Women Voters guide, he wrote: "A clear separation of church and state should be a guiding principle".

Statement or interview

Curriculum and the role of teachers. He has spoken about keeping politics out of the curriculum and about the place of teachers in writing the standards. After his 2024 win, he said in the San Antonio Report: "We need to make sure to develop a curriculum that focuses on academics, focuses on pedagogy, and really steps away from politics and personal beliefs."

The Texan reported that in a September 2026 interview he called teacher input on the standards an "afterthought" or a "box to check" and described the process as "altered and diminished". In the same Texan account, he said: "I'm not an educator, and I would never call myself an educator."

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

In 2024 he wrote that uncertified teachers should be allowed in some cases, and that voucher funds should not go to programs led by uncertified teachers. When the League of Women Voters asked whether uncertified teachers should be allowed in Texas classrooms, he answered: "In some cases, yes. Districts should have the option to rely on non-certified educators for hard-to-fill subjects."

His condition was that "an emergency certification should be followed by proper certification within a certain amount of time". His opponent answered "No" in the same guide.

In his San Antonio Report questionnaire that year he added: "We also must make sure that voucher funds are not spent on programs led by uncertified teachers."

Voting record

He voted against allowing every charter applicant that came to a named roll call in 2025 and 2026 except Unidos Soccer Leadership Academy. He voted against seven named applicants. He voted against allowing six of them, from Mater Academy San Antonio in April 2025 to Texas High School for Accelerated Learning in June 2026, and the board allowed all six. He voted to veto the seventh, Valenta Academy, and the board vetoed it 10-3-1. In committee he also voted no on the 2026 Generation 31 list, which carried 10-4.

The exception was Unidos, which he voted to allow in committee on June 25, 2025, a motion defeated 5-9. On June 27, 2025, he voted not to veto it, and the board vetoed it 9-4-1.

On the social studies standards he voted no all seven times they came to a recorded vote, from September 2025 to June 2026, two of them as reported by the Tribune, and all seven passed. He also voted no on the 2026 reading list, on removing all Houghton Mifflin Harcourt products from the approved list and on the January 2025 motions to strike or reject parts of the engineering career-course standards.

On the American Indian/Native Studies course, he voted yes in committee, no on postponing it and yes on suspending the rules to take it up. On training for school trustees, he voted no on the parental-rights rule at first reading in January 2026 and was absent for the substitute package in April 2026.

His individual votes on certification rules are not recorded. He was not on the School Initiatives committee for its January, April and November 2025 votes, and the board minutes give no names.

How to read this document

Scope. This document covers the Democratic winners of Texas's statewide races, the State Board of Education and the Texas Supreme Court, as requested. At the requester's direction on November 9, 2026, it adds the U.S. senator-elect and the two sitting State Board Democrats who were not on the ballot. It leaves out the winners for two courts: the Court of Criminal Appeals, which hears criminal cases only, and the Fifteenth Court of Appeals.

The Fifteenth Court is new. Senate Bill 1045 of 2023 gave it "exclusive intermediate appellate jurisdiction" over cases brought by or against state agencies, among them the Texas Education Agency, the state agency that oversees public schools. The law applies to appeals perfected on or after September 1, 2024, and on that date it also moved to the new court the cases of that kind pending in other courts of appeals that had been filed on or after September 1, 2023.

Result status. The Associated Press has called every race here except State Board District 8. Nothing is certified: the canvass, the state's official count, ends on December 7, 2026. The record in this document runs to November 9, 2026.

Kinds of evidence.

  • A pledge is a promise about future conduct.
  • A statement is something the person said or wrote, dated, with the venue.
  • A social media post is quoted from the platform named.
  • A recorded vote is printed in the House or Senate Journal or in State Board minutes.
  • An authored bill is one the person filed, with its outcome.
  • An official act is a vote or action in a prior office, such as a school board.
  • A court ruling is given with the judge's role, the question and the outcome.
  • A backer is an endorsement, contribution or independent expenditure, with the election stage.

Three rules matter most. A pledge is not policy. A vote on a large bill is a vote on the bill, not on each provision. And a court ruling is not a policy view.

The floor-vote tables taken from the House and Senate Journals name the stage at which each vote was taken. Second reading is first approval, and third reading is final passage in that chamber. Concurrence in House or Senate amendments is one chamber accepting the other's changes, and a conference report (some tables say conference committee report) is the final negotiated version.

Party comparisons. Some vote tables note that most members of the person's party in that chamber, or on the State Board, voted the other way. The note comes from our own count of the roll call in the journal or minutes. It lets you see where a person's vote differed from most of their party's, though we do not give exact counts.

How sources appear. Links sit in the text. A quotation or record with no qualifier was confirmed on the linked page. Where an item is credited to a news outlet, or carries "according to" or "as reported by", it comes from a news account or other secondary source.

What "no public record" means. Where a search of the named sources returned nothing and the gap matters, as with teacher residencies or a judge's views on education, the text says there doesn't appear to be a public record of the person's statements on the subject. The tables say it more briefly, as "None found" or the like. Either form means we searched those sources without result. It does not mean the person has no view.

Limits. We could not read posts on X, Facebook and Instagram for most people here, and some news pages, aggregator sites and Ballotpedia questionnaires could not be opened. The section near the end, Not confirmed, and sources that could not be opened, lists those sources along with the items we could not confirm. The State Board minutes record individual votes for only some decisions, and most show only "carried" or a tally.

Looking ahead. The section "Implications for the future" gives our estimates of what will happen next, and the section "How we made the estimates" gives the rules and sources behind them. Everything else in this document is record.

How we made the estimates

This section gives the definitions, dates, rules and sources behind the estimates in "Implications for the future", while the winners' own words and votes are in the profiles. These two sections are the only parts of this document that look ahead.

What the five words mean

Our estimates use five words, each tied to a date:

  • very likely: we would be surprised if it did not happen
  • likely: we expect it to happen, with real doubt
  • uncertain: we see no clear lean either way
  • unlikely: we expect it not to happen, with real doubt
  • very unlikely: we would be surprised if it happened

These are our estimates as of November 9, 2026, and no source offers odds.

What the dates mean

"By May 31, 2027" means passed by both chambers before the regular session ends, and the constitution limits that session to 140 days. After it ends, the governor can call special sessions under article IV, section 8: "The Governor may, on extraordinary occasions, convene the Legislature".

The budget is the one law both chambers must pass every two years, so the two parties must agree on it. The governor can then strike items from it. Under article IV, section 14 of the constitution, the governor "may object to one or more of such items, and approve the other portion of the bill". That line-item veto removes an item of spending, but it cannot repeal a program or change an amount.

June 20, 2027 is the governor's deadline to veto bills passed at the end of the session, which article IV, section 14 sets at "twenty days after such adjournment".

The Senate adopts its rules when the session opens on January 12, 2027, and under its current rules, 16 senators can change them.

20 rows

Our firmest estimates concern what one office can do alone or what current law already requires.

The rules and evidence behind each estimate

The Senate's rules and the lieutenant governor. The Associated Press had called every statewide race here for the Democrats by November 9, 2026. That day the MultiState tracker projected that they would hold the House and Republicans the Senate.

So the first changes are the ones an office can make alone: appointments subject to Senate consent, agency decisions, audits, vetoes and choices about what to argue in court. New laws that Senate Republicans oppose are unlikely to pass.

Republicans are likely, by January 31, 2027, to cut the power over committees and bills held by the lieutenant governor, who presides over the Senate. The outgoing lieutenant governor, Dan Patrick, urged that cut on November 9, 2026. Every estimate that needs the Senate depends on the outcome. If the lieutenant governor keeps her powers after the Senate votes on its rules in January 2027, those estimates become less firm. The section "Texas Legislature" gives the projected seats in each chamber, the votes each action takes and the comparable cases.

Vouchers and education savings accounts. All six winners who served in the Legislature voted against Senate Bill 2 of 2025 when it came to a vote in the House or the Senate. The bill created the education savings accounts, and Hinojosa has pledged to end them.

The Legislature is very unlikely to repeal the law by May 31, 2027, since the Senate majority that passed the program remains. After the election the Tribune reported that Paul Bettencourt, the Republican senator who led its passage, now says the Legislature should review the 2026-27 results.

Arizona is a comparable case. The 74 reported that Governor Katie Hobbs's first-year attempt to repeal the universal part of her state's program "went nowhere" against Republican lawmakers, and the Houston Chronicle reported that she then worked with them on accountability.

As comptroller, Eckhardt is very likely to keep the program running through the 2026-27 school year and to audit it, by August 31, 2027. Chapter 29 of the Education Code says the comptroller "shall establish and administer" the program and requires a private firm to audit it yearly. The comptroller alone writes the program's rules, sets its application deadlines and suspends providers that break them.

On June 10, 2026, the comptroller reported more than 102,000 students awarded accounts. In November the Tribune put participation at roughly 110,000, which is a different measure.

Whether the budget includes money for the program in fiscal years 2028 and 2029 is uncertain, by June 20, 2027. Under §29.3521 the Legislature must set each two-year amount, so House budget writers and the Senate both affect it, and so does the governor's line-item veto, as the Texas Tribune described it. We do not estimate an amount.

What to watch: the six repeal bills filed on November 9, 2026, House Bills 164, 646, 675 and 735 and Senate Bills 106 and 294. None is yet in committee.

School funding and teacher pay. Hinojosa, Goodwin and Talarico voted for House Bill 2 of 2025 in the House at second reading, third reading and concurrence, on April 16, April 17 and May 29, 2025. Rosenthal voted no on the final version.

The raises in House Bill 2 are very likely to stay funded by June 20, 2027, because §48.158 requires districts to keep paying them.

A new across-the-board raise is uncertain by the same date. The Senate is not a known opponent of raises, since it passed House Bill 2 31 to 0. The open questions are revenue and what each chamber asks in return. Hinojosa's campaign site pledges higher teacher pay but names no dollar figure.

Revenue sets the limit. Under article III, section 49a of the constitution, "No bill containing an appropriation shall be considered as passed or be sent to the Governor for consideration until and unless the Comptroller of Public Accounts endorses his certificate thereon showing that the amount appropriated is within the amount estimated to be available". The same section lets four-fifths of each chamber override that limit in an emergency. The certificate concerns available money, not policy.

So the comptroller's revenue estimate in January 2027 will affect the estimates on voucher money, a new raise and preparation funding.

What to watch: the first House budget, and the bills filed on November 9, 2026, on the basic allotment, the state's base funding per student.

Testing, accountability and state takeovers. Hinojosa, Goodwin, Talarico and Rosenthal in the House, and Johnson in the Senate, voted against House Bill 8 of 2025, which replaced STAAR, the state test. The profiles record each vote. The Senate passed the bill 21 to 5, so a law that cancels its new tests or pauses the A-F ratings, the state's letter grades for schools, is very unlikely by August 31, 2028.

Pausing the ratings without a new law is also very unlikely by then. House Bill 8 requires ratings to be public "not later than August 15 of each year" and allows "Not Rated" only in listed cases, such as a declared disaster. So Hinojosa's pledge to pause the system needs a new law, or it fits only those cases.

The commissioner can change the standards or measures behind the ratings under §39.0541, and with a commissioner Hinojosa chose in office, such a change is likely by August 31, 2028. Authority does not show intent. House Bill 8 also sets a deadline: standards not adopted by the July 15 before a school year leave that year's ratings "based on the performance standards in effect for the preceding school year".

A commissioner chosen by Hinojosa, confirmed or serving while the Senate considers the nomination, is likely to run the agency by May 31, 2027. Article IV, section 12 of the constitution, which governs the governor's appointments, does not mention an acting appointment. It says only that one made during a session "shall be with the advice and consent of two-thirds of the Senate present", under article IV, section 12(b).

The appointment of the current commissioner, Mike Morath, expires January 10, 2027, as Texas Public Radio, KPRC and the Houston Chronicle reported, though the statute gives no date. Hinojosa can name an acting commissioner immediately, according to the Texas Tribune's reading of the law.

Whether the Senate confirms her nominee by May 31, 2027 is uncertain. Confirmation takes 21 of the 31 senators if all attend, and the Texas Tribune reported on November 5, 2026, that Democrats hold 12 seats on projected results. So at least nine Republicans must vote yes.

A minority of senators has blocked nominees before. Senate Democrats blocked Secretary of State David Whitley in 2019, according to The Week. The National Center for Science Education reported that the Senate rejected Don McLeroy as State Board chair in 2009.

If the Senate votes on Hinojosa's nominee for commissioner between January and May 2027, under §7.051, that vote will affect the estimates on who runs the agency, confirmation, the ratings and charter vetoes.

Hinojosa pledged to return Houston's school district to its elected board. The commissioner's letter of May 30, 2025 extended the authority of the state-appointed board of managers "until June 1, 2027", and promised: "On or around June 1, 2027, I will announce the transition timeline for the return of elected trustees to the district's governing board".

The state is very likely to announce a timeline for returning Houston's elected trustees by December 31, 2027. Elected trustees are very unlikely to hold all the board's seats by then. The commissioner's Houston announcement, promised in the agency's letter, will affect both Houston estimates.

What to watch: the nominee's hearing before the Senate Nominations Committee, which hears appointees first, and the field test of the new tests on February 1 to 5, 2027.

Charter schools. The people covered here split on charter schools. Talarico wrote in 2022 that high-quality nonprofit charters have a role, while Goodwin, Rosenthal, Mallet-Fontenot, Palmer, Van de Walker and Reveles have asked for fewer new charters or a pause. There doesn't appear to be a public record of a charter pledge in Hinojosa's 2026 campaign.

A binding pause needs a law, so the Legislature is very unlikely to pass one by May 31, 2027. Without a law, the commissioner can still propose fewer new charters, and the commissioner alone approves expansions of existing ones. Under §12.114, "A revision of a charter of an open-enrollment charter school may be made only with the approval of the commissioner".

The State Board of Education votes only on the new charters the commissioner proposes. Under §12.101(b-0), each one takes effect unless, within 90 days, "a majority of the members of the board present and voting vote against the grant".

Whether the board vetoes more of them by December 31, 2027 is uncertain. On named roll calls in 2025 and 2026, Clark and Reveles voted against nearly every applicant, as the board minutes show. Pérez-Díaz voted to allow several after calling for a halt in 2018.

The Texas Tribune reported that, as of November 5, 2026, each party held seven seats, with District 8 not called. That race decides which party has eight of the 15 seats, though not how any member votes. Dana Van de Walker led there by 564 votes on the Secretary of State's count of November 4, 2026, and the canvass, the state's official count, should settle the race. Its result will affect the charter-veto and curriculum estimates.

What to watch: the District 8 result when the canvass ends by December 7, 2026, under a Secretary of State advisory, and the next commissioner's charter decisions.

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools. Hinojosa in the House and Johnson in the Senate voted against Senate Bill 10 of 2025, which requires the Ten Commandments to be displayed in classrooms. Johnson said as a candidate that he would not defend the law because he considers it unconstitutional, and KTRE reported that he would not defend it while appeals continue.

The Legislature is very unlikely to repeal that law, or the library laws, House Bill 900 of 2023 and Senate Bill 13 of 2025, by May 31, 2027, because repeal needs the Senate.

With Johnson as attorney general, his office is likely to stop arguing in court that the Ten Commandments law is constitutional by December 31, 2027. That would not repeal or suspend the law. Schools must still comply unless a court blocks it, and Senate Bill 10 still makes defending sued schools a duty of the office. Court rulings are outside these estimates.

The State Board's 2026 social studies standards and its reading list with Bible stories stay unless a board majority votes to reopen them. Whether it does by December 31, 2027 is uncertain, and it depends on who wins District 8.

What to watch: the attorney general's filings in those appeals once Johnson takes office, and the District 8 result.

Teacher preparation and certification. There doesn't appear to be a public record of a statement on teacher residencies, routes built around a supervised year in a classroom before certification, from any of the 20 people here. Nor does there appear to be a public record of a pledge from Hinojosa that names a certification rule, program or funding source.

The rules come from the State Board for Educator Certification, and the governor appoints its 11 voting members with Senate consent, under chapter 21 of the Education Code. The State Board of Education can reject a certification rule, but not change it, by two-thirds of members present and voting within 90 days, under §21.042.

Since there doesn't appear to be a public record of any pledge on certification rules, a substantial change in the rules is unlikely by December 31, 2027. That silence is not evidence that nothing will change: the estimate rests on who sits on the certification board in 2027.

The teacher-preparation allotment in House Bill 2, described in a Texas Education Agency presentation, is very likely to be funded as designed for fiscal years 2028 and 2029, by June 20, 2027. Every winner who voted on the bill voted for it at least once, in the House or the Senate, and there doesn't appear to be a public record of any group opposing the funding.

What to watch: the February 1, 2027 expiry of a third of the certification board's seats under §21.034, and Hinojosa's nominees. Members whose successors are not confirmed may stay until the 2029 regular session ends, under article XVI, section 17.

Higher education. A Texas Tribune guide republished by High Plains Public Radio reported that Hinojosa plans to appoint university regents who would extend tuition grants to housing, food, transportation and textbooks.

Repeal of Senate Bill 17 of 2023, on diversity offices, or Senate Bill 37 of 2025, on faculty governance, is very unlikely by May 31, 2027. It needs the Senate, as the Texas Tribune described. Regents need the votes of two-thirds of senators present under the constitution, and we make no estimate on those appointments because we found too few comparable cases.

What to watch: the regents' seats that expire in February 2027, 11 according to KBTX and 20 according to the Tribune.
